title: Green Banking & Sustainable Finance
tagline: Read climate risk like a credit risk, screen deals for environmental and social harm, and build green products that stand up to scrutiny.
sectors: Islamic banks and Islamic banking windows
description:
Floods, heatwaves and wildfires have turned climate change from a distant debate into a balance-sheet event for banks everywhere. Crops, warehouses, roads and branches go under water, borrowers who never missed an instalment fall behind, export buyers demand carbon data, and boards ask a new question: **how exposed are we, and what are we doing about it?**

This certification gives credit, risk, compliance, branch and product staff the practical answers. You will learn to tell **physical risk** from **transition risk**, apply ESG thinking to real borrowers, work through **environmental and social due diligence** and the A/B/C risk categories used by the IFC Performance Standards and the Equator Principles, and see how supervisors from Lagos to Beijing, Brasília and Karachi expect banks to manage these risks.

You will then put numbers on climate risk with scenario and stress-testing methods, design and verify **green products** such as solar and energy-efficiency financing, test green bonds and sukuk for greenwashing, calculate a bank's own **scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions**, connect sustainability to Islamic finance principles, and plan the disclosures and the green banking unit that pull it all together.

Every stage uses real cases from around the world. Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic international banking scenarios.
audience: Credit analysts, relationship managers and credit approvers in corporate, SME and agriculture lending
Risk managers who run portfolio analysis, stress tests and risk reporting
Compliance officers and green banking or ESG unit staff
Branch managers and product managers designing or selling retail, SME and agri products
Islamic banking staff, Shariah compliance teams and treasury staff working on sukuk
Internal auditors who review environmental and social risk controls
outcomes: Explain how climate change creates credit, market, operational, liquidity and reputational risk for banks
Classify physical and transition risks and apply ESG and double-materiality thinking to borrowers in any market
Carry out environmental and social due diligence using international standards, assign A/B/C categories and set practical action plans and covenants
Use scenario analysis and simple stress-test calculations to show how climate shocks change expected credit losses
Design, verify and report green loans, green bonds and green sukuk while avoiding greenwashing
Calculate a bank's scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, including a simple financed-emissions estimate
Plan climate disclosures, align sustainability with Islamic finance principles and set up a green banking unit

quest.name: The Tidewater Mandate
quest.premise: Months after record floods, Banyan Bridge Bank's farm loans in the delta are sliding into default, and a European buyer has told one of its biggest garment clients to cut carbon or lose orders. The board in Singapore gives Dr Amara Okafor a mandate: build a green banking unit that sees climate risk coming. You are her first recruit. With Mei Lin Tan, Arif Rahman, Layla Haddad and a sceptical Rodrigo Alves, clear five stages from Sylhet to Lagos, then face the final boss: the board itself.

badge.name: Tidewater Mandate Holder
badge.description: Awarded to bankers who can price climate risk, screen deals for harm, build credible green products and report it all honestly.

cast.name: Dr Amara Okafor
cast.role: Head of the new Green Banking Unit, Singapore, your mentor

cast.name: Arif Rahman
cast.role: Relationship Manager, Corporate Banking, South Asia

cast.name: Layla Haddad

sessions.title: Why Climate Is a Banking Risk
sessions.summary: The floods left a line on the wall of every branch in the delta. Learn how climate change turns into defaults, damaged collateral and lost business, how physical and transition risks differ, and how ESG thinking helps you read a borrower.
objectives: Explain how a climate event such as a major flood travels into a bank's credit, operational, liquidity and reputational risk
Distinguish acute and chronic physical risks from policy, technology, market and reputational transition risks, and recognise liability risk
Apply ESG and double-materiality thinking to borrowers in any market
Describe why banks in low-emitting countries still face transition risk through export buyers, investors and border carbon rules

cards.title: The line on the wall
cards.setting: Banyan Bridge Bank, Sylhet branch, north-east Bangladesh. A brown water mark runs across the wall at shoulder height.

lines.text: The floods receded months ago, but the mark on the branch wall is still there. So is the pile of overdue loan files on the manager's desk.
Tea gardens, two rice mills, a fish farm, a fertiliser dealer. All good payers before the rains. Now half of them can't even reach their land.
(on video from London) Floods are an act of God, Arif. We reschedule, we wait, it passes. I don't see why the board wants a whole new unit for this.
(joining from Singapore) Because it will not pass, Rodrigo. Extreme rain, heatwaves and water stress are getting more frequent. A risk that keeps coming back is a risk you have to model.
And it's not only water. Our biggest denim client in Dhaka just got an email from its European buyer: share your carbon footprint and a reduction plan, or we move orders.
Two different problems hitting the same balance sheet. That's why I asked for you. Welcome to the Green Banking Unit, our first recruit.
Stage one is the High-Water Mark. By the end of it you should be able to explain to Rodrigo exactly how a flood or a buyer's email becomes a bad loan.

cards.title: How a flood becomes a bad loan

scenes.heading: The hazard
scenes.narration: It starts with the weather: weeks of extreme rain, or a glacial lake that bursts high in the mountains. On its own, that is a natural event. It becomes a banking event when it reaches the bank's customers.

scenes.heading: Borrowers lose income
scenes.narration: Crops rot, livestock die, factories close and roads wash away. Borrowers lose the cash flow they planned to repay from, so the probability that they default goes up.

scenes.heading: Collateral loses value
scenes.narration: Land, warehouses and stock that secure the loans are damaged or become hard to sell. If a borrower does default, the bank recovers less. That is a higher loss given default.

scenes.heading: Second-round effects
scenes.narration: A tractor dealer in the next town may stay dry, but his farmer customers stop buying. Suppliers, traders and shops far from the water feel the shock through the local economy.

scenes.heading: The bank feels it everywhere
scenes.narration: Branches close and systems go down, which is operational risk. Depositors withdraw savings to rebuild, which is liquidity risk. Rising bad loans eat into profits and capital.

scenes.heading: And people are watching
scenes.narration: How a bank treats flood-hit borrowers, and what it finances next, shapes its reputation with customers, regulators and investors. Climate risk is not a new risk type. It is a driver of the risks you already manage.

cards.title: Real case: Pakistan's 2022 floods
cards.caption: Rounded figures from widely reported official and international estimates after the 2022 monsoon floods. Use them for context, not as precise data.

items.label: Of Pakistan under water at the peak
items.detail: Sindh and Balochistan were hit hardest, with farmland flooded for months.

items.label: People affected
items.detail: Homes, livelihoods, schools and health facilities were damaged or lost.

items.label: Estimated damage and losses
items.detail: Post-flood assessments put combined damage and economic losses at around this level.

items.label: Pakistan's share of global emissions
items.detail: A country that emits little can still be among the most exposed to climate impacts.

cards.title: Physical and transition risk
cards.body:
Climate-related financial risk comes in two main families.

**Physical risk** comes from the climate itself:
- **Acute:** sudden events such as floods, heatwaves, cyclones, wildfires and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Himalaya or the Andes.
- **Chronic:** slow shifts such as rising average temperatures, changing rainfall, falling groundwater, glacier retreat and sea-level rise pushing salt water into deltas like the Mekong.

**Transition risk** comes from the move to a low-carbon economy:
- **Policy and legal:** carbon pricing, efficiency rules, or carbon charges at the border such as the EU's CBAM on imports like cement, steel, aluminium and fertilisers.
- **Technology:** cheaper solar or electric vehicles making older assets uneconomic.
- **Market:** buyers and investors demanding low-carbon products.
- **Reputation:** being seen to finance harm.

A third strand, **liability risk**, arises when people sue for climate or pollution harm, or for misleading disclosure.

cards.title: Acute, chronic or transition?
cards.prompt: Sort each item from Mei Lin's risk register into the type of climate risk it describes.

items.text: A glacial lake bursts and sweeps away a hydropower contractor's site camp in the Himalaya
A week-long heatwave forces a poultry farm outside Lagos to shut down
Seawater creeps further up the Mekong delta each year, making rice land too salty
Average summer temperatures keep rising, cutting wheat yields year after year
Groundwater in a dry valley keeps falling, raising pumping costs for apple orchards
A European buyer requires measured carbon data from a Dhaka spinning mill
Cheap rooftop solar makes a fuel-oil power plant's electricity hard to sell
A border carbon charge raises the cost of a cement maker's exports to Europe

cards.question: A shrimp farm in the Mekong delta finds that each year the land floods a little more often at high tide and the soil grows saltier. Which kind of climate risk is this mainly?
options: Acute physical risk
Transition risk from new regulation
Chronic physical risk
Liability risk
cards.explanation: A slow, year-on-year shift such as rising sea levels and salinity is chronic physical risk. Acute risk is a sudden event like a cyclone or a single flood. Nothing here involves policy, technology or a lawsuit.

cards.title: Two families of climate risk
cards.caption: Many borrowers face both at once. A textile mill can lose a season to floods and a buyer to carbon rules.

items.label: Comes from
items.left: Weather events and long-term climate shifts
items.right: Policy, technology, market and reputation changes on the way to low carbon

items.label: Typical timing
items.left: Can strike any year; chronic effects build over decades
items.right: Builds with policy and market shifts, sometimes suddenly

items.label: Most exposed
items.left: Agriculture, food processing, coastal and riverside property, water-hungry industry
items.right: Cement, steel, fertiliser, fossil-fuel power, exporters to carbon-conscious markets

items.label: Hits the bank through
items.left: Defaults, damaged collateral, branch outages, deposit withdrawals
items.right: Falling borrower margins, stranded assets, lost export orders, reputation

items.label: Loan tenor lens
items.left: Even a one-year crop loan faces the next rainy season
items.right: Long-tenor loans live long enough for rules and technology to change

cards.title: Rodrigo's question
cards.setting: Group head office, Marina Bay, Singapore. Amara's new team room still has unopened boxes.

lines.text: (on video from London) Fine, floods hurt farmers. But transition risk? Most of our borrowers are in countries that barely emit anything. Let Europe worry about carbon.
Their emissions are small, but our exporters sell into markets that care. Garments go to brands with carbon targets. Cement and fertiliser can face carbon charges at the EU border.
And money is moving too. Foreign lenders and investors now ask what we finance. Being in a small-emitting country does not protect a borrower from a buyer's rules.
So what am I supposed to do, stop lending to every factory with a chimney?
No. You read the borrower better. That's what ESG is for: environmental, social and governance factors that change how risky a client really is.

cards.title: ESG and double materiality
cards.body:
**ESG** is a lens for factors that ordinary financial analysis can miss:
- **Environmental:** emissions, energy, water, waste, effluent, exposure to climate hazards.
- **Social:** labour conditions, health and safety, child labour, community impacts, land acquisition, customer treatment.
- **Governance:** board independence, related-party dealings, ownership transparency, controls, ethics.

ESG is not charity. It asks which factors can change cash flows, collateral or reputation.

**Double materiality** means looking both ways:
- **Outside-in:** how climate and ESG issues affect the borrower (and so the bank). Example: rising energy costs squeeze a mill's margin.
- **Inside-out:** how the borrower affects people and the environment. Example: a dyeing unit's effluent harms a village canal.

Inside-out impacts often become outside-in risks later, through fines, protests, lost buyers or lawsuits.

cards.title: Name that idea
cards.prompt: Link each term to the example from Amara's training file that best illustrates it.

pairs.right: A new fuel-oil power plant that cannot compete once cheaper solar and stricter rules arrive, long before its loan is repaid.
A tannery's untreated waste water damages crops and health in the villages downstream.
Higher gas prices and a buyer's carbon rules squeeze a spinning mill's profit margin.
A family group's chairman also signs off large purchases from companies owned by his brothers.
A fertiliser dealer's shop is dry, but sales collapse because his farmer customers lost their crops.

cards.front: Myth: climate is an environmental topic, not a credit topic.
cards.back: Fact: climate events and policies change borrowers' cash flows and collateral, which is exactly what credit analysis measures.

cards.front: Myth: last season's floods were a one-off.
cards.back: Fact: extreme heat and rain are expected to become more frequent and intense, so a bank should plan for repeat events, not a single shock.

cards.front: Myth: only big corporates are exposed.
cards.back: Fact: small farmers, SMEs and microfinance borrowers often have the least cushion and suffer first.

cards.front: Myth: ESG means refusing every polluting client.
cards.back: Fact: the usual aim is to price and manage the risk and help clients improve. Exclusion is kept for the most harmful activities.

cards.front: Myth: transition risk is a rich-country problem.
cards.back: Fact: exporters, foreign-funded projects and carbon-intensive sectors in low-emitting countries feel buyers', investors' and border rules directly.

cards.title: The road to green finance
cards.caption: Global milestones for context. Countries build on them at different speeds, so always check the rules where you work.

items.label: UN climate convention
items.detail: The UNFCCC is agreed at the Rio Earth Summit, the basis for later global climate deals.

items.label: Equator Principles
items.detail: Project finance banks adopt a shared environmental and social risk framework built on IFC standards.

items.label: Paris Agreement
items.detail: Countries commit to hold warming well below 2°C and to set national climate targets (NDCs).

items.label: TCFD and NGFS
items.detail: The TCFD publishes its four-pillar disclosure framework; central banks form the NGFS to work on climate risk.

items.label: ISSB standards
items.detail: The ISSB issues IFRS S1 and S2, a global baseline for sustainability and climate disclosure.

items.label: EU CBAM begins
items.detail: The EU's carbon border mechanism starts a reporting-only phase; financial charges phase in from 2026.

cards.title: The first board note
cards.situation: The board has asked Amara for a one-page note on the floods. Rodrigo has drafted a line: 'The floods were an exceptional event. Affected loans have been rescheduled and no further action is needed.' Amara asks what you would put in its place.

choices.text: Keep Rodrigo's line. Rescheduling is the standard tool and the board does not want alarm.
choices.outcome: The note goes out and nothing changes. Next rainy season, the same districts flood and the same borrowers default, now with rescheduled balances on top. The board asks why nobody saw it coming. Rescheduling eases one event; it does not measure repeat exposure.

choices.text: Recommend stopping all new agriculture lending in the flood-hit region until the climate settles down.
choices.outcome: The board likes the caution but asks how long 'until it settles' is. It will not settle. Farmers lose access to credit when they most need it to rebuild, and the bank exits a core market without measuring which districts and crops are actually most exposed.

choices.text: Propose mapping the portfolio by district and sector against flood and heat hazards, and building the results into credit decisions and limits.
choices.outcome: The board approves. Within weeks you can show which districts, sectors and collateral carry the most physical risk, and the credit committee starts asking climate questions on new deals. This treats climate as a recurring driver of credit risk, which it is.

choices.text: Suggest a glossy sustainability report highlighting the bank's flood relief donations.
choices.outcome: The report gets good press for a week. But it says nothing about the bank's exposure, and investors notice the gap. Donations are welcome; they are not risk management.

cards.title: Real case: PG&E and the California wildfires (2019)
cards.body:
**What happened:** Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E), California's largest utility, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in **January 2019**. It cited potential liabilities of **more than USD 30 billion** from deadly wildfires in 2017 and 2018, including the 2018 Camp Fire, which official investigators linked to its power lines.

**Why bankers study it:**
- **Physical risk:** hotter, drier conditions lengthened the fire season and raised the stakes of every equipment failure.
- **Liability risk:** the losses came mainly through claims from victims, insurers and local governments, not through damage to PG&E's own assets.
- **Credit risk:** an investment-grade utility became a bankruptcy case within about two years.

Many commentators called it one of the first major corporate failures linked to climate change. PG&E emerged from bankruptcy in 2020 after agreeing settlements with wildfire victims.

**Lesson:** a 'safe' borrower can be undone when a climate hazard meets legal liability.

cards.question: In 2011, months of flooding in Thailand shut major industrial estates north of Bangkok. Car and electronics makers in Japan, the US and elsewhere had to cut output for lack of parts. For a bank lending to one of those distant manufacturers, what does this show?
options: A transition risk caused by new carbon rules
An indirect, second-round effect of a physical climate event
A governance failure at the manufacturer
Nothing climate-related, because the manufacturer's own factories stayed dry
cards.explanation: The manufacturers were hit through their supply chains: the floods stopped their Thai suppliers. That is a second-round effect of physical risk. A borrower does not need to be under water, or even in the same country, to be hit.

cards.title: One client, two climate risks
cards.body:
**Gazipur Indigo Mills** (fictional), near Dhaka, makes denim for export and borrows USD 15 million from Banyan Bridge.

**Physical:** floods hit its cotton supply and the roads to the port, prices jumped, margins shrank and the working capital line was drawn to the limit. Part of the yard flooded, damaging stock held as collateral.

**Transition:** its largest European buyer wants a measured carbon footprint, a plan to cut emissions and evidence of water treatment. Without them, about a third of orders could move to a competitor.

**What Mei Lin does:**
- Asks for the mill's energy use, fuel mix and water treatment details.
- Checks how much revenue depends on the demanding buyer.
- Notes that a rooftop solar and efficient-boiler upgrade could cut both costs and emissions, a lending opportunity, not just a risk.

One borrower, two risk families, and one conversation that helps both sides.

cards.title: Ask the climate question early
cards.body:
In your next credit call, add three plain questions:
- **Where** are your sites, stock and suppliers, and have they flooded or overheated before?
- **Who** buys from you, and are they asking about carbon, water or labour?
- **What** would a bad rainy season or a 30% jump in energy costs do to your cash flow?

Write the answers in the credit memo. Most clients appreciate a banker who understands their real risks.

cards.question: Mei Lin argues that Banyan Bridge should look at climate in both directions for every large borrower. Which pair best shows the two directions of double materiality?
options: How heat and floods could hurt the borrower's business, and how the borrower's emissions and effluent affect people and nature
How the borrower's profits compare with peers, and how its share price has moved
How the borrower treats its staff, and how it treats its customers
How climate affects the bank's branches, and how it affects the bank's head office
cards.explanation: Double materiality pairs the outside-in view (climate and ESG issues affecting the borrower) with the inside-out view (the borrower's impact on people and the environment). The other pairs look in only one direction or at ordinary financial comparisons.

cards.title: High-Water Mark reached
items: Climate is not a separate risk type; it drives credit, operational, liquidity, market and reputational risk you already manage.
Physical risk is acute (floods, heatwaves, GLOFs) or chronic (heat, water stress, sea-level rise). Transition risk is policy, technology, market or reputation.
Liability risk arises when people sue over climate or pollution harm or misleading disclosure.
Floods raise defaults, cut collateral values and spread through supply chains to borrowers who stayed dry.
ESG reads environmental, social and governance factors that change a borrower's risk; double materiality looks outside-in and inside-out.
A small national share of emissions does not protect exporters and carbon-intensive borrowers from buyers' and border rules.

cards.prompt: Pick one borrower or customer segment you know well. Which physical risk and which transition risk could hurt it most over the next five years, and what would be the first sign in its account?

quiz.question: A glacial lake outburst flood destroys a mountain hotel financed by your bank overnight. How is this climate risk best classified?
options: Chronic physical risk
Acute physical risk
Transition risk from technology change
Liability risk
quiz.explanation: A sudden, event-driven disaster such as a GLOF is acute physical risk. Chronic risk builds slowly over years, such as rising temperatures or sea-level rise. No policy, technology or legal claim is involved.

quiz.question: A Dhaka spinning mill's main buyer in Europe says it will move orders unless the mill shows measured carbon data and a reduction plan. Which risk does this create for the mill's lender?
options: Acute physical risk, through extreme weather
Transition risk, through market pressure from buyers
Chronic physical risk, through long-term climate change
Liability risk, through a lawsuit
quiz.explanation: Buyers demanding low-carbon supply is a market-driven transition risk: the mill could lose revenue as the economy shifts. Nothing physical has happened to the mill, and nobody is suing it.

quiz.question: Floodwater damages a cotton warehouse that secures a ginner's loan, and its sale value falls sharply. The ginner has not yet missed a payment. Which credit measure has worsened most directly?
options: Probability of default, because collateral damage always causes the borrower to default
Exposure at default, because the loan amount has increased
None, because the ginner is still paying
Loss given default, because the bank would recover less if the ginner defaulted
quiz.explanation: Damaged collateral means the bank would recover less after a default, so loss given default rises. The probability of default may also rise if cash flows suffer, but the collateral damage hits recoveries directly. The loan amount has not changed.

quiz.question: A dyeing unit discharges untreated waste water into a canal used by nearby villages for irrigation. Under double materiality, this is mainly an example of:
options: An outside-in risk of climate change on the borrower
An inside-out impact of the borrower on people and the environment
A chronic physical climate risk
A technology transition risk
quiz.explanation: Inside-out means the borrower's effect on the outside world, here on villagers and the canal. It can later turn into an outside-in risk for the borrower through fines, closure orders or lost buyers.

quiz.question: A bank has a 15-year loan to a new fuel-oil power plant. Five years in, cheaper solar and tighter rules mean the plant runs only a few days a month and cannot cover its debt. What has the plant become?
options: A second-round effect
A stranded asset
An acute physical risk
A green asset
quiz.explanation: A stranded asset loses its economic value before the end of its expected life because of transition forces such as cheaper technology or new policy. That is the case here, long before the loan is repaid.

quiz.question: Over the past decade, seawater has moved steadily further up the Mekong delta, and rice land that secures several agri loans is becoming too salty to farm. How should this be classified?
options: Acute physical risk
Chronic physical risk
Market transition risk
Reputational risk only
quiz.explanation: A slow, persistent change such as sea-level rise and salt intrusion is chronic physical risk. Acute risk is a sudden event. The damage to collateral value is a direct physical effect, not mainly a reputation issue.

quiz.question: A family-owned food group has no independent directors, and its chairman approves large purchases from firms owned by his relatives. In an ESG review, which pillar does this weakness fall under?
options: Environmental
Social
Governance
None, because it is a purely commercial matter
quiz.explanation: Board independence and related-party dealings are governance issues. They matter to a lender because weak governance can hide losses or divert cash away from the company that owes the bank.

quiz.question: A colleague in a country that emits little says: 'We produce under 1% of global emissions, so transition risk does not apply to our borrowers.' What is the best response?
options: Exporters and carbon-intensive borrowers still face buyers', investors' and border carbon rules in the markets they sell to
He is right, because transition risk mainly follows national emissions, and a share this small is too low for buyers or investors to act on
He is right for now, but only until his own government introduces a carbon tax
Transition risk applies only to banks, not to borrowers
quiz.explanation: Transition risk follows markets and money, not just national emissions. A cement or garment exporter selling to carbon-conscious buyers can lose orders or pay border charges whatever its home country's share of emissions.

quiz.question: Villagers file a court case against a chemical plant claiming its emissions damaged their health, and also name the bank that financed the plant's expansion. Which strand of climate and environmental risk does the court case represent?
options: Chronic physical risk
Technology transition risk
Liability risk
Acute physical risk
quiz.explanation: Liability risk arises when parties seek compensation for environmental or climate harm, or for misleading disclosure. The claim may also create reputational risk, but the lawsuit itself is liability risk.

quiz.question: After the floods, a motorcycle dealer in a town that stayed dry starts missing instalments because his customers, mostly farm families from nearby flooded villages, have stopped buying. What does this show?
options: The dealer's problem cannot be climate-related, because his own showroom and stock were never touched by the floodwater
This is a transition risk caused by a shift away from fertiliser
Physical climate events spread to borrowers through second-round effects in the local economy
The bank should treat this purely as a governance failure by the dealer
quiz.explanation: The dealer's income depended on flood-hit customers, so the physical shock reached him indirectly. Banks must look beyond direct damage to supply chains and customer bases.

sessions.title: Regulatory Expectations and Environmental and Social Due Diligence
sessions.summary: A USD 5 million tannery expansion lands on your desk with a Friday deadline. Learn the international standards behind environmental and social risk management, how supervisors in different countries apply them, and how to screen, categorise, condition and monitor a deal.
objectives: Describe the IFC Performance Standards and Equator Principles, and the three strands common to national green banking frameworks
Explain how environmental approvals work, from a lighter screening-level review to a full EIA, and why the competent authority differs by country
Run the E&S due diligence process: exclusion screening, A/B/C categorisation, due diligence, action plan, approval and monitoring
Write practical conditions and covenants and respond correctly when a borrower breaches them

cards.title: The Friday deadline
cards.setting: Banyan Bridge corporate centre, Chennai, India. Arif drops a thick credit proposal on your desk at 4:40 pm on a Tuesday.

lines.text: Kaveri Leather Works. Twenty years with us, never late. They want USD 5 million to add two new processing lines. The client wants approval by Friday.
(on video from Singapore) Tannery means chrome, effluent and a lot of water. Where's the environmental approval for the new lines? I can only see the one for the old plant.
Come on, Mei Lin. They've had that approval for years. The new lines are on the same plot.
Same plot, double the capacity, double the effluent. This is exactly what our E&S screening exists for. It is also what our supervisors and our own lenders expect of us.
(by text from London) Amara, please don't lose me a twenty-year client over paperwork.
Nobody wants to lose the client. We want a deal that doesn't blow up at the plant or in our audit. Let's walk through the Screening Gate properly and still be fast.

scenes.heading: A shared global standard
scenes.narration: Most bank E&S systems trace back to the IFC Performance Standards: eight standards covering pollution, labour, community health, land, biodiversity, indigenous peoples and cultural heritage.

scenes.heading: The Equator Principles
scenes.narration: Since 2003, banks that adopt the Equator Principles apply these standards to project finance. More than a hundred financial institutions have signed up, and they use the same A, B and C risk categories.

scenes.heading: National frameworks
scenes.narration: Supervisors then set their own rules. Nigeria's sustainable banking principles and China's green credit guidelines date from 2012, Brazil's central bank rule from 2014, and Pakistan's green banking guidelines from 2017.

scenes.heading: Three common strands
scenes.narration: Most of these frameworks share three strands: manage E and S risk in what the bank finances, grow green business, and shrink the bank's own footprint.

scenes.heading: Governance and reporting
scenes.narration: They also expect a board-approved policy, a dedicated function, trained staff and regular reporting, both to the board and to the supervisor.

scenes.heading: Check the rules where you work
scenes.narration: Scope, thresholds and reporting formats differ by country and change over time. Before you quote a detail, check the current rules with your compliance team.

cards.title: The E&S due diligence path
cards.caption: Proportionate effort: a category C working capital line moves through in minutes, a category A project takes weeks.

items.label: Screen against exclusions
items.detail: Is the activity on the bank's exclusion list? If yes, decline. No conditions can fix it.

items.label: Categorise A, B or C
items.detail: Judge the likely scale and reversibility of environmental and social impacts.

items.label: Due diligence
items.detail: Permits, site visit, questionnaire, past incidents, consultant reports where needed.

items.label: Action plan and covenants
items.detail: Agree an E&S action plan with deadlines and put key items into the facility documents.

items.label: Approve with conditions
items.detail: Credit approval records the category, findings and conditions.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Periodic reports, site visits and escalation if the borrower falls behind.

cards.question: Banyan Bridge replaces diesel generators at 40 branches with solar panels and batteries. Of the three strands common to national green banking frameworks, which does this mainly support?
options: Environmental and social risk management
Green business facilitation
Own-impact reduction
Shariah compliance
cards.explanation: Cutting the bank's own energy use and emissions falls under own-impact reduction. E&S risk management concerns the bank's borrowers, and green business facilitation concerns products the bank offers customers.

cards.title: Categories A, B and C
cards.body:
Categorisation, used in the IFC standards and the Equator Principles, sets how much due diligence a deal needs. Judge the **likely impacts of the activity being financed**, not the client's reputation.

| Category | Typical impacts | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **A** (high) | Significant, diverse, irreversible or unprecedented | Large dam with resettlement; greenfield cement plant with a new quarry |
| **B** (medium) | Limited, site-specific, largely reversible, manageable with known measures | Expanding a dyeing unit; a mid-sized hospital |
| **C** (low) | Minimal or none | Software house; trading company working capital |

Two rules of thumb:
- **Scope matters.** An existing tannery borrowing for a new office is different from one doubling its processing lines.
- **When in doubt, go up.** If impacts are uncertain, choose the higher category and let due diligence prove otherwise.

Every deal, even category C, is first checked against the **exclusion list**.

cards.title: Categorise the pipeline
cards.prompt: Sort each financing request in this week's pipeline into the E&S category it should most likely receive.

items.text: A new hydropower dam in a mountain valley that will resettle four villages
A greenfield cement plant in Egypt with a new limestone quarry
A large coastal land reclamation project for a new housing city in West Africa
Adding a dyeing line, with effluent treatment, to an existing textile unit near Dhaka
Building a 60-bed private hospital in Nairobi that will generate medical waste
Expanding a poultry farm from four sheds to eight
A working capital line for a software exporter in Bengaluru
Trade finance for a mobile phone distributor in Dubai
Fit-out of a consultancy firm's rented office in Singapore

cards.title: Lighter review or full EIA?
cards.caption: Names differ: Pakistan uses IEE and EIA, the EU's EIA Directive lists projects that always need a full assessment and screens others case by case, and India splits approvals between national and state bodies. Check the local rules.

items.label: What it is
items.left: A screening-level examination (in Pakistan, an IEE)
items.right: Environmental impact assessment: a full, detailed study

items.label: Used for
items.left: Projects with limited, manageable impacts
items.right: Projects with potentially significant impacts

items.label: Public consultation
items.left: Often not required
items.right: Generally required before a decision

items.label: Approval by
items.left: The competent environmental authority, often with conditions
items.right: The competent environmental authority, often with conditions

items.label: Banker's job
items.left: Confirm approval covers this project and its conditions are met
items.right: Same, plus check consultation and mitigation commitments

cards.title: What the site visit showed
cards.setting: Kaveri Leather Works, a leather cluster in Tamil Nadu. The smell reaches the car before the gate does.

lines.text: Arif and you walk the plant with the owner's son, Karthik. The old effluent treatment plant hums in a corner.
That treatment plant was sized for the old capacity. Where will the waste water from two extra lines go?
And this pipe behind the drum yard: it bypasses the treatment plant and runs straight to the drain. Is it in use?
Karthik goes quiet. Nearby, two young workers are moving wet, chrome-tanned hides with bare hands.
(on the phone) Okay, I didn't know about the pipe. But they're good people. Can we still do this deal?
Maybe. Not as written. First tell me exactly what you found, then let's decide what a responsible approval looks like.

cards.title: The Kaveri decision
cards.situation: Kaveri Leather Works (category B) wants USD 5 million for two new lines. Findings: environmental approval covers only the old capacity; the treatment plant is too small for the expansion; a bypass pipe sends some effluent to the public drain; workers handle chrome-tanned hides without gloves. The family is willing to fix things but wants funds quickly. What do you recommend to the credit committee?

choices.text: Approve now. The family has a 20-year clean repayment record and has promised to fix the issues.
choices.outcome: The money goes out and the lines start up on the old treatment plant. Six months later the state pollution regulator seals the plant after a complaint, and the bank's best client cannot operate or repay. A promise is not a control: nothing tied the money to the fixes.

choices.text: Decline. The bypass pipe shows the client cannot be trusted.
choices.outcome: The bank avoids this risk, but Kaveri borrows from a lender that asks no questions, and the effluent keeps flowing. Declining is reasonable for an excluded activity or a client that refuses to change; here the client is willing, and the problems can be fixed with known measures.

choices.text: Approve with an action plan: seal the bypass and get approval for the new capacity before first drawdown, tie tranches to treatment upgrades, require protective gear, and monitor.
choices.outcome: The committee approves. The pipe is sealed within a week, approval for the expansion is obtained, and the treatment upgrade is verified before the second tranche. The client keeps its bank, the drain runs cleaner, and the bank's exposure is protected by conditions it can enforce.

choices.text: Approve, and ask the client to sign a letter confirming it complies with all environmental laws.
choices.outcome: The client signs. The letter is false the day it is signed, and the bank knew it. If the plant is sealed, the letter will not recover a single dollar, and an examiner will ask why the bank ignored its own site visit findings.

cards.title: Real case: Rana Plaza, Bangladesh (2013)
cards.body:
**What happened:** on 24 April 2013 the Rana Plaza building in Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed. It housed several garment factories making clothes for international brands. **More than 1,100 workers died** and thousands more were injured. Cracks had appeared in the building the day before, yet workers were told to return.

**What followed:** more than 200 brands signed the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, which funded independent inspections of thousands of factories and required repairs.

**Why lenders study it:**
- **Social risk is life-and-death risk.** Building safety, fire exits and the right to refuse unsafe work belong in E&S due diligence.
- **Buyers act after a disaster.** Brands demanded inspections and cut suppliers that failed them, which hit those suppliers' cash flow.
- **Permits are not proof.** Ask who checked the structure and what happens when a worker raises an alarm.

cards.back: Eight international standards for managing environmental and social risk in projects, from labour and pollution to land, biodiversity and indigenous peoples.
A framework, launched in 2003, that signatory banks use to apply the IFC standards and A/B/C categories to project finance.
Activities the bank will not finance at all, such as forced or harmful child labour, trade in banned chemicals or protected wildlife, or anything illegal under local law.
An agreed list of fixes, each with an owner, deadline and evidence of completion, attached to the credit approval.
Something that must be done before the bank releases money, for example obtaining environmental approval for the new capacity.
An ongoing promise in the facility documents, such as complying with environmental standards and reporting incidents, with consequences for breach.
Legal limits on effluent, emissions and noise set by national or local law. Treatment plants are judged against them.
Releasing a loan in stages, each unlocked by verified progress, so the bank keeps leverage until the fixes are done.

cards.question: A request comes in to finance a trading company whose main line is importing a pesticide that is banned in its own country, relabelled for sale. The company is profitable and offers full collateral. What should the E&S screening produce?
options: A decline, because the activity is on the exclusion list and no conditions can make it acceptable
Category B with an action plan to phase out the product within two years
Category C, because a trading company has no factory and no direct impacts
Approval with a higher profit rate to reflect the extra risk
cards.explanation: Exclusion screening comes first. Trading a banned chemical is illegal and harmful, so the deal is declined regardless of collateral or pricing. Categories and action plans only apply to activities that are not excluded.

cards.title: The social side and the law
cards.body:
E&S due diligence is not only about smoke and effluent. Look for:
- **Labour:** child labour, unpaid or below-minimum wages, forced overtime, and freedom to raise grievances.
- **Health and safety:** building safety, protective equipment, chemical handling, fire exits, boiler safety.
- **Community:** land acquisition and resettlement, access to water, dust and traffic, and whether affected people were consulted.

**Who approves depends on where you are:**
- Some countries use one national agency.
- Others split the work: in India, state pollution control boards issue consents to operate; in Pakistan, environment moved to the provinces in 2010, so each has its own EPA.
- In the EU, national authorities apply a common EIA Directive.

You are not the regulator. Your job is to confirm the borrower holds the approvals it needs from the **competent authority** for **this** project, and is meeting their conditions.

cards.title: The monitoring loop
cards.caption: Monitoring is where most E&S programmes fail. Approval is the start, not the finish.

items.label: Borrower reports
items.detail: Periodic E&S report against the action plan, with evidence such as test results and photos.

items.label: Bank reviews
items.detail: E&S officer checks progress, deadlines and any incidents or complaints.

items.label: Site visit
items.detail: Risk-based visits: more often for category A and for B deals with open actions.

items.label: Act on findings
items.detail: Agree corrections, escalate breaches, adjust the risk rating or hold disbursements.

cards.title: When monitoring finds a breach
cards.prompt: Three months after approval, a visit finds the bypass pipe at Kaveri Leather Works has been reopened. Put the bank's response in the right order.
steps: Record the evidence: photos, location, date and who was present
Raise it formally with the borrower and ask for an explanation
Escalate to the E&S officer and credit approver under the bank's policy
Hold further disbursements while the breach remains open
Agree a corrective action with a short, fixed deadline
Verify the fix on a follow-up visit before releasing the hold

cards.title: Real case: India's tannery pollution ruling (1996)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in *Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India* (1996), India's Supreme Court heard complaints that tanneries in Tamil Nadu were releasing untreated effluent, polluting rivers, farmland and drinking water.

**What the court did:** it confirmed that the **precautionary principle** and the **polluter pays principle** are part of Indian environmental law. It directed that polluting tanneries install treatment or face closure, and that affected people be compensated.

**Why it matters to a banker:**
- Courts and regulators can close non-compliant plants, turning a pollution problem into a repayment problem overnight.
- 'Polluter pays' means clean-up and compensation costs land on the borrower's cash flow.
- Effluent treatment sized for the real capacity is not a nice-to-have; it is a condition of staying in business.

Similar principles appear in many legal systems, so check how they apply where you work.

cards.title: Red flags in an E&S file
cards.body:
- An environmental approval for a **different capacity, location or product** than the one being financed.
- An approval that has **expired** or whose conditions are not mentioned anywhere.
- A consultant's report that reads like a **template**, or is signed by the borrower's own staff.
- **No grievance channel** for workers or neighbours, or complaints that nobody can explain.
- Pressure to skip a site visit "because the client is old and trusted".

Any one of these is a reason to ask more, not a reason to decline.

cards.question: A borrower building a new industrial estate in an Indian state shows Arif an environmental approval issued years ago by a national agency for an earlier, smaller version of the project. Why should the E&S officer look more closely?
options: Approvals from national agencies are always invalid, so the project must be declined
The approval must come from the authority that is competent for this project today and must cover the project actually being financed
Approvals are only needed for category C projects
There is no issue, because approvals never expire or need updating
cards.explanation: Which authority approves a project differs by country and can change, and an approval for a smaller, earlier project may not cover the current one. An old approval is not automatically invalid, but it needs checking, not declining by reflex.

cards.title: Screening Gate passed
items: The IFC Performance Standards and the Equator Principles set the international baseline, including A/B/C categories.

National frameworks (Nigeria and China 2012, Brazil 2014, Pakistan 2017) share three strands: E&S risk management, green business and own-impact reduction, plus board policy, a dedicated function and reporting.
Screen every deal against the exclusion list first, then categorise A, B or C by the impacts of the activity financed.
Confirm the environmental approval comes from the competent authority, covers this project and that its conditions are met; rules differ by country, so check locally.
Turn findings into an action plan with conditions precedent, covenants and tranches, then monitor and escalate breaches.

cards.prompt: Think of a client in your own portfolio. If you walked its site tomorrow, what would you look at first, and which condition would you want in place before the next disbursement?

quiz.question: Which set correctly lists the three strands common to many national green banking frameworks, such as Pakistan's 2017 guidelines?
options: Carbon pricing, renewable energy targets for each bank, and compulsory annual green bond issuance
Credit risk, market risk, and operational risk
Exclusion lists, A/B/C categories, and site visits
Environmental and social risk management, green business facilitation, and own-impact reduction
quiz.explanation: These frameworks combine managing E&S risk in financing, growing green business and reducing the bank's own footprint. Exclusion lists and categories are tools within the first strand, not separate strands.

quiz.question: A new hydropower dam will flood a valley and require resettling four villages. How should it most likely be categorised for E&S due diligence?
options: Category B
Category A
Category C
Excluded
quiz.explanation: Large-scale resettlement and irreversible changes to a valley are significant, diverse and largely irreversible impacts, which is category A. Dams are not automatically excluded; they need the deepest due diligence.

quiz.question: Arif says a working capital line for a software exporter is category C, so the bank can skip E&S screening altogether. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, because category C deals sit outside the bank's E&S framework entirely
Software exporters are always category A, because of the electricity used by their servers and offices
Category C deals need a full environmental impact assessment
Every deal is first checked against the exclusion list, even if it ends up as category C
quiz.explanation: Exclusion screening applies to all financing before categorisation. A category C deal needs little further due diligence, but it still passes through the screen.

quiz.question: In tiered environmental assessment systems, such as Pakistan's IEE and EIA, what is a key difference between the lighter review and a full EIA?
options: An EIA is a full study for higher-impact projects and generally needs public consultation; the lighter review is a screening-level examination
The lighter review is prepared and approved by the lending bank, while an EIA is approved by the environmental authority
An EIA is only needed for projects paid for by foreign lenders
The lighter review is required for every bank loan above a set size, whatever the activity, while an EIA is only for government projects
quiz.explanation: Both are reviewed by the competent environmental authority. The EIA is the fuller assessment for higher-impact projects and generally involves public consultation; the lighter review suits projects with more limited impacts.

quiz.question: A textile unit in an Indian state wants to expand. India splits environmental approvals between national and state bodies. Which body should the bank expect to see on the factory's approval?
options: The environmental authority that is competent for this kind of project in that state
The central bank
Whichever environmental authority the borrower prefers to apply to
The borrower's bank
quiz.explanation: Where approvals are split between national and state or provincial bodies, the bank checks that the approval comes from the authority competent for that project and place. The central bank regulates banks, and banks only check that approvals exist.

quiz.question: In Kaveri Leather Works' approval, the bank requires environmental approval for the new capacity to be obtained before any money is released. What is this requirement called?
options: An exclusion
A covenant waiver
A post-disbursement review
A condition precedent
quiz.explanation: A condition precedent must be met before disbursement. It gives the bank maximum leverage because no money moves until it is satisfied.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of an E&S action plan (ESAP) attached to a credit approval?
options: To replace the borrower's environmental approval once the bank is satisfied with the project
To calculate the profit rate on the loan
To record the bank's own carbon emissions
To set out specific fixes with owners, deadlines and evidence, so the bank can track and enforce them
quiz.explanation: An ESAP turns due diligence findings into concrete, time-bound actions. It works alongside regulatory approvals; it does not replace them.

quiz.question: A monitoring visit finds that a poultry farm with an undrawn tranche has started dumping waste from its sheds into a stream used by a nearby village, against its action plan. What should the bank do after recording the evidence?
options: Raise it formally with the borrower and escalate internally, holding further disbursements while the breach is open
Release the next tranche promptly, so that the borrower has enough funds available to fix the waste problem and avoid a default
Report the borrower to the media
Do nothing until the next annual review
quiz.explanation: The bank documents, raises the breach with the borrower, escalates under its policy and uses its leverage by holding disbursements until a verified fix. Releasing money first removes that leverage.

quiz.question: A colleague quotes, from memory, an exact loan size above which the national supervisor requires full E&S due diligence. What is the best practice before relying on it?
options: Check the current regulatory rules and the bank's own E&S policy, because thresholds and requirements are updated
Use the figure, because supervisory thresholds never change once issued
Ignore all thresholds and apply full environmental and social due diligence to every retail, consumer and small business loan
Ask the borrower what threshold applies
quiz.explanation: Supervisory rules on E&S risk are updated over time and differ by country, and the bank's policy may be stricter. Always confirm the current requirement before relying on a remembered figure.

quiz.question: During a site visit, workers at a tannery are handling chrome-tanned hides without gloves, and a 14-year-old is working on the drum floor. Which part of E&S due diligence do these findings belong to?
options: Only the environmental side, because chrome is a chemical
The social side: occupational health and safety, and child labour
Governance, because the board should have stopped it
None, because labour issues are outside a bank's E&S review
quiz.explanation: E&S due diligence covers labour and health and safety as well as pollution. Unsafe chemical handling and a child on the factory floor are serious social findings, and harmful child labour is on typical exclusion lists.

sessions.title: Climate Risk in Credit: Scenarios and Stress Tests
sessions.summary: Rodrigo wants numbers, not adjectives. Learn how climate fits into each step of the credit cycle, how scenario analysis differs from a stress test, and how to show what a flood or a carbon charge does to expected losses, collateral cover and interest cover.
objectives: Build climate questions and adjustments into origination, rating, pricing, collateral, monitoring and portfolio limits
Explain the difference between scenario analysis and stress testing, and the four broad families of climate scenarios
Calculate how climate shocks change expected loss, collateral coverage and interest cover
Use proxies and ranges sensibly when borrower data is missing, and turn results into management action

cards.title: Show me the numbers
cards.setting: Board risk committee prep, 14th floor, Banyan Bridge's London office. Rain hammers the windows.

lines.text: Amara, your stage one note was well written. But the risk committee doesn't fund adjectives. How much could climate cost us? In dollars.

We can't predict the future, but we can test it. If the floods come back to the same six districts, what happens to our agri losses? If Europe charges our cement client for carbon, can it still pay interest?
And you'll pull those numbers out of thin air?
Out of the same tools you use every day: probability of default, loss given default, exposure, collateral cover, interest cover. We just change the assumptions.
Welcome to the Stress Chamber. Let's give Rodrigo his dollars, and be honest about what they can and can't tell him.

cards.title: Scenarios, stress tests and four possible futures

scenes.heading: Scenario analysis
scenes.narration: A scenario is a plausible story about the future, not a forecast. Scenario analysis asks: if the world went this way, how would our borrowers and our portfolio fare? It usually looks years or decades ahead.

scenes.heading: Stress testing
scenes.narration: A stress test applies a severe but plausible shock and measures the damage, often over a shorter horizon. Could we absorb a repeat of last year's floods in the same districts next year?

scenes.heading: Orderly
scenes.narration: In an orderly future, climate policy starts early and tightens gradually. Transition costs are real but manageable, and physical damage stays lower.

scenes.heading: Disorderly
scenes.narration: In a disorderly future, action comes late and suddenly. Carbon prices and rules jump, and carbon-heavy borrowers are hit hard and fast.

scenes.heading: Hot house world
scenes.narration: In a hot house world, policies stay weak. Transition risk is low, but heat, floods and water stress keep getting worse. Physical risk dominates.

scenes.heading: Too little, too late
scenes.narration: The worst mix: action comes late and is not enough. The bank faces sharp transition costs and severe physical damage at the same time.

cards.title: Four climate futures
cards.caption: The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), a group of central banks and supervisors formed in 2017, frames climate scenarios this way. Most banks test at least one high-transition and one high-physical case.

items.label: Hot house world
items.detail: Weak policy, low transition risk, severe physical damage.

items.label: Too little, too late
items.detail: Late, insufficient action: high transition and high physical risk.

items.label: Orderly
items.detail: Early, gradual action: both risks kept relatively low.

items.label: Disorderly
items.detail: Late, sudden action: high transition risk, physical risk contained.

cards.question: Rodrigo wants to know what would happen if governments did little more on climate for decades. Which scenario family should Mei Lin use, and which risk will dominate?
options: Hot house world, where physical risk dominates
Disorderly, where transition risk dominates
Orderly, where both risks stay low
Too little, too late, where only transition risk matters
cards.explanation: Weak policy for decades describes a hot house world: transition pressure stays low while heat, floods and water stress keep worsening, so physical risk dominates.

cards.title: Expected loss, climate-adjusted
cards.body:
Banks estimate **expected loss (EL)** as:

**EL = PD × LGD × EAD**
- **PD:** probability of default over the period.
- **LGD:** share of the exposure lost if default happens (after recoveries).
- **EAD:** the amount owed at default.

Climate moves each part:
- Floods or carbon costs cut cash flow, so **PD rises**.
- Damaged or hard-to-sell collateral in a flood zone means **LGD rises**.
- Borrowers draw their credit lines harder in a crisis, so **EAD can rise**.

**Worked example (delta agri book):** EAD USD 50 million, PD 2%, LGD 40%.
- Baseline EL = 50m × 0.02 × 0.40 = **USD 0.4 million**.
- Flood stress: PD 6%, LGD 55% → 50m × 0.06 × 0.55 = **USD 1.65 million**.

The stressed loss is about four times the baseline. That is the number the committee remembers.

cards.title: Mei Lin's flood stress test
cards.caption: Illustrative results for the six most flood-exposed districts. All figures are assumptions for the exercise.

items.label: Baseline expected loss
items.detail: EAD 50m × PD 2% × LGD 40%.

items.label: Stressed expected loss
items.detail: PD rises to 6% and LGD to 55% after a repeat flood.

items.label: Warehouse collateral cover
items.detail: A 25% flood-zone haircut on a USD 30m warehouse securing a USD 25m loan.

items.label: Agri book in six districts
items.detail: A concentration that turns one bad flood season into a portfolio problem.

cards.title: Climate in every step of the credit cycle
cards.prompt: Match each stage of the credit cycle to the climate action Amara wants built into it.

pairs.right: Ask where sites, stock and suppliers are and whether buyers demand carbon or water data.
Apply a climate overlay that can move the borrower's internal grade up or down a notch.
Map the security's location against flood and heat hazards and apply a haircut or require insurance.
Use rainfall alerts and heatwave warnings as early-warning triggers to contact exposed borrowers.
Set concentration limits by district and sector so one hazard cannot sink a large share of the book.

cards.title: Real case: the ECB's 2022 climate stress test
cards.caption: Rounded figures from the European Central Bank's published results (July 2022). The ECB itself said the losses were likely an underestimate.

items.label: Banks in the exercise
items.detail: Directly supervised euro-area banks answered questions on their climate stress-testing capabilities.

items.label: Lacked a robust framework
items.detail: Roughly six in ten banks did not yet have a climate stress-testing framework ready to use.

items.label: Projected losses for 41 banks
items.detail: Credit and market losses under a disorderly transition and short-term flood and drought scenarios.

items.label: Income from carbon-heavy clients
items.detail: Share of banks' interest income from non-financial corporates earned from greenhouse-gas-intensive industries.

cards.title: Rodrigo's favourite client
cards.setting: Corporate banking floor, London. Rodrigo has printed Nile Ridge Cement's annual report and underlined the export page.

lines.text: Nile Ridge Cement, out of Egypt. EBITDA USD 50 million, interest of USD 12 million. Over four times cover. You won't find a safer name.
Their export plan sends 400,000 tonnes a year to Europe. Each tonne of cement carries roughly 0.8 tonnes of CO₂ in our assumption.
If the importer has to pay a carbon charge and passes it back as a lower price, what does that do to Nile Ridge's cash flow?
The European buyers pay it, not Nile Ridge.
Buyers who pay more will either cut the price they offer or buy from a cleaner supplier. Either way, it lands on Nile Ridge. Let me run it.

cards.title: A carbon charge meets interest cover
cards.body:
Mei Lin's **disorderly-transition** test for Nile Ridge Cement (all figures are assumptions):

- Exports to Europe: **400,000 tonnes** of cement a year.
- Embedded emissions: **0.8 t CO₂ per tonne** → 400,000 × 0.8 = **320,000 t CO₂**.
- Assumed carbon cost absorbed by Nile Ridge: **USD 100 per t CO₂** → 320,000 × 100 = **USD 32 million** a year.

**Interest cover (EBITDA ÷ interest):**
- Today: 50m ÷ 12m = **4.2×**.
- Stressed: (50m − 32m) ÷ 12m = 18 ÷ 12 = **1.5×**.

A 'safe' borrower drops close to the bank's comfort limit. That does not mean decline. It means talking to Nile Ridge now about cutting emissions per tonne, for example through waste-heat recovery, alternative fuels or blended cement, and about whether to shift export markets.

cards.title: What to do with the six districts
cards.situation: Mei Lin's stress test shows that 35% of the agri book sits in six flood-prone districts, and a repeat flood would roughly quadruple expected losses there. The risk committee asks what management will do.

choices.text: Stop all new lending in the six districts immediately.
choices.outcome: Losses from new lending stop growing, but the bank abandons good farmers when they need rebuilding finance, loses market share to competitors and still holds the existing book. It treats the result as a verdict rather than a guide.

choices.text: Set district concentration limits, require crop insurance or takaful where available, finance adaptation such as raised storage and better irrigation, and price for the higher risk.
choices.outcome: The committee approves. Over two seasons, concentration falls, more loans carry insurance or takaful cover and some farmers move stock to raised warehouses. The bank keeps serving the market while cutting both probability of default and loss given default.

choices.text: Ignore the results, because the model contains too many assumptions to be trusted.
choices.outcome: Every model is uncertain. Ignoring it means the next flood hits an unchanged book. Uncertainty is a reason to show ranges and test assumptions, not to throw the analysis away.

choices.text: Raise provisions on every agri loan across the group by 50% straight away.
choices.outcome: The profit hit is large and lands on districts with little flood exposure as well. Provisioning should follow the bank's accounting policy and evidence on specific exposures, not a blunt number unrelated to the test.

cards.title: Top-down or bottom-up?
cards.caption: Many banks start top-down to find hot spots, then go bottom-up on the largest exposed borrowers.

items.label: Starts from
items.left: Sector and region averages applied to the whole portfolio
items.right: Individual borrowers' own financials, sites and emissions

items.label: Data needed
items.left: Low: exposure by sector and district
items.right: High: borrower-level data and engagement

items.label: Strength
items.left: Fast, covers everything, finds concentrations
items.right: Precise, captures borrower-specific mitigants

items.label: Weakness
items.left: Misses differences between borrowers
items.right: Slow and costly; usually only for large exposures

cards.title: Real case: Peabody Energy and stranded coal (2016)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in **April 2016** Peabody Energy, then the largest US coal producer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Several other big US coal miners had already filed in 2015 and 2016.

**The drivers, as widely reported:**
- US power companies switched from coal to cheaper natural gas and, increasingly, renewables.
- Environmental rules on power plants tightened.
- Coal prices fell, while Peabody carried heavy debt, much of it from a large Australian acquisition in 2011.

Peabody emerged from bankruptcy in 2017 with much less debt; lenders and bondholders took large losses along the way.

**Why it matters for scenario work:** the forces that strand assets (cheaper technology, policy and market shifts) build over years. A loan of 10 to 15 years needs a scenario horizon that long. A one-year stress test would never have shown it.

cards.title: Running a climate scenario exercise
cards.prompt: Put the steps of Mei Lin's first climate scenario exercise in a sensible order.
steps: Agree the purpose and scope with management: which portfolios and which questions
Choose the scenarios and the time horizon
Identify the most exposed sectors, districts and borrowers using a heat map
Translate each scenario into borrower impacts on revenue, costs and collateral
Estimate changes in PD, LGD and expected loss
Report results with ranges and recommend management actions

cards.question: A warehouse valued at USD 40 million secures a loan of USD 32 million. Because it sits in a flood zone, the bank applies a 30% haircut to the value. What is the collateral cover after the haircut?
cards.explanation: Haircut value = 40m × (1 − 0.30) = 28m. Cover = 28m ÷ 32m = 87.5%. Before the haircut, cover was 40 ÷ 32 = 125%. A loan that looked over-secured is now under-secured.

cards.front: No emissions data from the borrower?
cards.back: Use a sector average per unit of output or revenue as a proxy, and mark it clearly as an estimate until real data arrives.
Collect the exact address or coordinates at the next review, so the site can be matched to flood and heat maps.
Run a range, such as low, central and high, and show the committee all three instead of one false-precision number.
Use recent events, such as Pakistan's 2022 floods or Thailand's 2011 floods, as an anchor: how did rescheduling and defaults move in affected areas?
Credit it: raised storage, insurance or takaful cover, or efficient equipment can lower PD or LGD in the analysis.

cards.title: Three ways to misuse a scenario
cards.body:
- **Treating it as a forecast.** A scenario says 'if', not 'will'. Present it as a what-if, never as next year's budget.
- **Showing one number.** Climate results are uncertain. Give a range and explain the main assumptions.
- **Stopping at the result.** The value is in the action: limits, pricing, insurance, engagement and new green lending. A test with no follow-up is just a report.

cards.question: Mei Lin wants a quick first view of which parts of a 40,000-loan SME portfolio are most exposed to heat stress, using only sector and district data. Which approach fits best?
options: A bottom-up analysis of every SME borrower's own financial statements
A top-down analysis applying sector and district averages across the whole portfolio
No analysis until every borrower provides emissions data
A single stress test of the bank's largest corporate borrower
cards.explanation: Top-down analysis uses averages by sector and region, needs little data and covers everything quickly, which suits finding hot spots in a large SME book. Bottom-up work on 40,000 borrowers would be slow and costly, and waiting for perfect data means no answer at all.

cards.title: Stress Chamber cleared
items: Scenario analysis explores plausible futures; a stress test applies a severe but plausible shock. Neither is a forecast.
Four scenario families, as framed by the NGFS: orderly, disorderly, hot house world, and too little, too late.
EL = PD × LGD × EAD. Climate can raise all three; show the stressed figure against the baseline.
Flood-zone haircuts can turn over-secured loans into under-secured ones; carbon costs can collapse interest cover.
Use top-down to find hot spots and bottom-up for the largest exposures; fill gaps with labelled proxies and ranges.
Results matter only when they drive action: limits, pricing, insurance or takaful, adaptation finance and client engagement.

cards.prompt: Choose one large exposure you know. What single assumption, such as a flood, a heatwave, an energy price jump or a carbon charge, would hurt it most, and roughly how would its interest cover or collateral cover change?

quiz.question: A crop finance portfolio has an exposure at default of USD 20 million, a probability of default of 3% and a loss given default of 50%. What is the expected loss?
options: USD 3 million
quiz.explanation: EL = PD × LGD × EAD = 0.03 × 0.50 × 20m = USD 300,000. Multiplying only PD by EAD gives USD 600,000, which ignores recoveries.

quiz.question: Floods damage the warehouses that secure a group of rice mill loans, making them hard to sell. Which part of the expected loss formula does this affect most directly?
options: Loss given default
Probability of default
Exposure at default
The discount rate
quiz.explanation: Collateral that is damaged or hard to sell reduces recoveries after default, which raises loss given default. Probability of default may also rise, but the collateral effect is on LGD.

quiz.question: What best describes the difference between scenario analysis and a stress test in climate risk work?
options: Scenario analysis is a forecast of what will happen to the bank, while a stress test is a rough guess used only when data is missing
A stress test is only for market risk, while scenario analysis is only for credit risk
They are two names for exactly the same exercise
Scenario analysis explores plausible futures over long horizons; a stress test applies a severe but plausible shock
quiz.explanation: Scenario analysis asks 'what if the world went this way?' across possible futures. A stress test applies a specific severe shock, often over a shorter period. Neither is a forecast.

quiz.question: In which scenario family does climate policy arrive late and suddenly, causing sharp transition costs while physical damage is kept relatively contained?
options: Disorderly
Orderly
Hot house world
Too little, too late
quiz.explanation: A disorderly scenario combines high transition risk from late, abrupt policy with lower physical risk. Too little, too late has high transition and high physical risk together.

quiz.question: A cement exporter is assumed to ship 100,000 tonnes a year to Europe, with 0.8 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne of cement and an absorbed carbon cost of USD 60 per tonne of CO₂. What is the annual carbon cost?
options: USD 6.0 million
USD 4.8 million
USD 48 million
quiz.explanation: Emissions = 100,000 × 0.8 = 80,000 t CO₂. Cost = 80,000 × 60 = USD 4.8 million. Using 100,000 tonnes without the 0.8 factor gives USD 6.0 million.

quiz.question: Which climate action belongs in the collateral step of the credit cycle?
options: Mapping the security's location against flood hazards and applying a haircut or requiring insurance
Setting a sector concentration limit for the whole portfolio
Asking the borrower at the first meeting whether its buyers require carbon or water data from their suppliers
Using rainfall alerts to call exposed borrowers
quiz.explanation: At the collateral step the bank checks where the security sits and adjusts its value or protection. Concentration limits are portfolio actions, buyer questions belong to origination, and alerts are monitoring tools.

quiz.question: A bank wants to understand precisely how a carbon charge would affect its five largest steel and cement borrowers, using their own plant data and financials. Which approach fits best?
options: A top-down analysis using sector averages
A survey of retail depositors
No analysis, because carbon charges apply only to foreign companies
A bottom-up analysis of those borrowers
quiz.explanation: Bottom-up analysis uses each borrower's own data and suits a small number of large, important exposures. Top-down averages would miss differences between these specific plants.

quiz.question: Mei Lin has no emissions data for 300 small textile borrowers. What is the most sensible way to include them in a transition-risk analysis?
options: Use sector-average emissions per unit of output or revenue as a clearly labelled proxy
Leave them out until each provides audited emissions data
Assume their emissions are zero
Copy the emissions figure of the largest textile borrower for all of them
quiz.explanation: A sector-average proxy, marked as an estimate, gives a reasonable starting picture. Leaving them out or assuming zero understates risk, and copying one large borrower's figure ignores differences in size.

quiz.question: A borrower's EBITDA is USD 30 million and annual interest is USD 10 million. A stress scenario adds USD 12 million of yearly energy and carbon costs. What is the stressed interest cover?
quiz.explanation: Stressed EBITDA = 30m − 12m = 18m. Interest cover = 18m ÷ 10m = 1.8×, down from 3.0×.

quiz.question: The risk committee is shown a single number: 'Climate will cost the bank USD 210 million in 2030.' What is the main weakness of this presentation?
options: It presents a scenario result as a precise forecast instead of a range based on stated assumptions
It is shown in US dollars instead of each country's local currency
It should have shown only physical risk, because transition risk cannot be measured in money with any accuracy
Committees should never see climate numbers
quiz.explanation: Scenario results depend heavily on assumptions and are not predictions. Good practice shows a range, explains the key assumptions and links results to actions.

sessions.title: Green Products, Green Bonds and Green Sukuk
sessions.summary: Risk is only half the mandate. Learn to design and verify green loans for solar, energy efficiency and green housing, understand how concessionary refinance and development-bank schemes work, and structure green bonds and sukuk that survive a greenwashing test.
objectives: Identify activities that qualify for green financing and the evidence needed to verify them
Explain how central bank refinance and similar concessionary schemes work in general terms and why their terms must be checked
Work out simple payback and affordability for solar and energy-efficiency loans
Apply the four core components of green bonds and sukuk and recognise common forms of greenwashing

cards.title: Queues at the Ikeja branch
cards.setting: Banyan Bridge, Ikeja branch, Lagos. 35°C, the grid keeps dropping and diesel for the generators has just gone up again.

lines.text: (visiting from Dubai) Every SME on this street is asking the same thing: can you finance solar? Their generator fuel bills have gone through the roof and outages kill their production.
(on video from Chennai) My corporate clients in Asia want it too. Rooftop solar, efficient motors, new boilers. I keep telling them we have nothing ready.
This is the other half of our mandate: finance the solution, not just measure the problem. Layla, can you build a product?
And while you're at it, the board wants a green sukuk next year out of Dubai. Every bank is talking about it. It'll look great in the papers.
It will look great only if every dollar goes where we say it goes. The Solar Bazaar is about building green products that are real, and proving it.

scenes.heading: Renewable energy
scenes.narration: Rooftop solar for homes, shops and factories, solar water pumps for farms, and larger wind or solar projects. The most familiar green loans in many markets.

scenes.heading: Energy efficiency
scenes.narration: Efficient motors, boilers, chillers, LED lighting and heat recovery. The client pays for the upgrade from the energy it saves.

scenes.heading: Green housing and buildings
scenes.narration: Homes and offices designed to use less energy and water: insulation, shading, solar-ready roofs and efficient fittings, ideally checked against a recognised green building standard.

scenes.heading: Clean transport
scenes.narration: Electric two- and three-wheelers, buses and vehicles, and efficient fleets for logistics firms.

scenes.heading: Water and waste
scenes.narration: Drip and sprinkler irrigation, effluent treatment, recycling and waste-to-value projects.

scenes.heading: Green needs proof
scenes.narration: A loan is only green if the money really buys the green asset. That means vendor checks, installation evidence and a record of the expected energy or emissions saved.

cards.title: Green or not green?
cards.prompt: Layla's team must tag the pipeline. Sort each request by whether it fits the bank's green lending criteria as described.

items.text: Rooftop solar for a sports goods factory in Lagos
Drip irrigation for an orchard in Kenya's Rift Valley
LED lighting and efficient chillers for a hospital in Dubai
Twenty electric three-wheelers for a transport cooperative in Dhaka
Three new diesel generators for a plastics factory, called 'green' because they replace older ones
Repainting a car showroom green and adding plants at the entrance
A new coal-fired boiler for a textile mill
General working capital for a company whose website says it 'loves the planet'

cards.title: How refinance schemes work
cards.body:
Central banks and development banks often use **concessionary refinance** or credit lines to push lenders towards priority sectors, including renewable energy. Pakistan and Bangladesh, for example, have run central bank refinance schemes for renewable energy and other green products.

**The typical mechanism:**
1. A bank lends to an eligible customer for an eligible purpose, such as a solar system.
2. The central bank or development bank provides cheap funding to the bank.
3. The bank lends on at a **capped end-user rate**, below normal market pricing.
