4. The bank still carries the **credit risk** and must follow the scheme's eligibility and documentation rules.

**Caution:** rates, limits, eligible technologies and even whether a scheme is open change over time and differ by country. Never quote a rate or limit from memory. Check the current scheme rules before advising a customer, and check that the bank has allocation available.

cards.question: Under a central bank refinance scheme for renewable energy, who bears the credit risk if a solar borrower defaults?
options: The lending bank
The central bank, because it provided the refinance
The solar vendor that installed the system
Nobody, because refinanced loans are guaranteed
cards.explanation: Refinance gives the bank cheaper funding so it can lend at a capped rate, but the bank still owns the loan and the credit risk. That is why normal credit assessment still applies to scheme loans.

cards.title: Solar loan maths for a Lagos SME
cards.caption: Illustrative figures in USD. Actual costs, savings and rates vary; check current fuel and grid tariffs, grid-export rules and pricing.

items.label: 10 kW system cost
items.detail: Panels, inverter, batteries, structure and installation from an approved vendor.

items.label: Monthly saving
items.detail: Based on the shop's past generator fuel and electricity bills and expected solar output.

items.label: Simple payback
items.detail: 8,400 ÷ 200 = 42 months, three and a half years.

items.label: Monthly instalment
items.detail: 80% financed (USD 6,720) over five years at an assumed 10% a year. Savings cover it.

cards.title: Verifying a solar loan
cards.body:
**Adeyemi Steel Works**, Lagos (fictional), wants USD 6,720 to finance 80% of a USD 8,400 rooftop system.

**Before approval, Layla's checklist:**
- Quotation from a vendor on the bank's approved list, with panel, inverter and battery model numbers.
- Past 12 months of fuel and electricity bills to size the system and estimate savings.
- Ownership or landlord consent for the roof.

**At disbursement:**
- Pay the **vendor directly**, not the customer, so the money cannot leak to other uses.

**After installation:**
- Installation certificate, geo-tagged photos and serial numbers matching the invoice.
- Grid-connection paperwork if relevant. Rules for selling power back to the grid are set by each country's energy regulator and are often revised (the UK closed its feed-in tariff to new applicants in 2019, for example), so check the current position before promising export income.

**Record the impact:** expected kWh generated a year, for the bank's green reporting.

cards.title: The 'green' generators
cards.setting: Layla's desk, Dubai. A voice note from a client plays on speaker.

lines.text: Bright Pack Plastics in Nairobi wants USD 9 million for new diesel generators. They say the new ones burn 15% less fuel, so it should go in the green book at the green rate.
Less diesel is still diesel. If we call that green, every polluter becomes green by buying a newer polluting machine.
Our sukuk needs a big pool of green assets, Layla. Five hundred million dollars doesn't fill itself.
And if the pool is stuffed with diesel generators, the first analyst who reads the report will call it greenwashing. Then the sukuk becomes our biggest reputational risk.
Let's set the rules first: what counts, how we pick, how we track the money, and how we report. Then we see how big the pool really is.

cards.title: Four core components of a green bond or sukuk
cards.caption: Market principles such as ICMA's Green Bond Principles (first published in 2014) share these four components, with external review strongly encouraged.

items.label: Use of proceeds
items.detail: Money goes only to eligible green projects with clear environmental benefits, defined in the framework.

items.label: Evaluation and selection
items.detail: A documented process and committee decide which projects qualify and how E&S risks are handled.

items.label: Management of proceeds
items.detail: Proceeds are tracked in a sub-account or register; unallocated funds held in stated liquid instruments.

items.label: Reporting
items.detail: Regular allocation reports (where the money went) and impact reports (what it achieved).

items.label: External review
items.detail: An independent second-party opinion before issue, and verification of allocation afterwards.

cards.title: Spot the greenwash
cards.prompt: Match each type of greenwashing to the example from Amara's file of claims the bank has rejected.

pairs.right: A loan marketed as 'eco-friendly financing' with no criteria for what it funds.
Promoting a factory's new solar roof while hiding that its untreated effluent still flows into a canal.
Calling new diesel generators green because they burn slightly less fuel than the old ones.
Claiming 50,000 tonnes of CO₂ avoided, with no data or method behind the number.
Moving old ordinary loans into the 'green pool' without checking they meet the criteria.

cards.title: Proceeds waiting for projects
cards.situation: Banyan Bridge issues a USD 500 million green sukuk. After six months, USD 360 million is allocated to verified eligible assets. Treasury proposes using the remaining USD 140 million for general corporate lending 'until the green pipeline catches up', and reporting later.

choices.text: Agree. Money is fungible, and investors only care about the final allocation.
choices.outcome: The mixed funds make tracking impossible. When the allocation report comes out, the reviewer cannot confirm what the unallocated money financed, and investors question the whole framework. Management of proceeds exists precisely to prevent this.

choices.text: Keep the USD 140 million tracked in the green register, hold it in the Shariah-compliant liquid instruments named in the framework, and disclose the 72% allocation and the plan to allocate the rest.
choices.outcome: Investors see exactly where the money is, the reviewer confirms the allocation, and the report is credible. Partial allocation is normal early on; transparency about it is what matters.

choices.text: Move existing car loans into the green pool so the sukuk shows 100% allocation.
choices.outcome: The pool looks full, but car loans are not eligible under the framework. This is relabelling, a classic form of greenwashing, and an external review would expose it.

choices.text: Return the USD 140 million to investors immediately to avoid any risk.
choices.outcome: This is cautious, but it breaks the sukuk's terms and gives up good projects that are coming through the pipeline. Transparent tracking and reporting solve the problem without unwinding the deal.

cards.title: Real case: Indonesia's sovereign green sukuk (2018)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in **March 2018** Indonesia issued a **USD 1.25 billion** five-year green sukuk, widely reported as the world's first sovereign green sukuk.

**How it was built:**
- A **green framework** set out eligible categories such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable transport, waste management and climate resilience.
- An **independent second opinion** reviewed the framework before issue.
- The government has published regular **allocation and impact reports** showing where the money went and what it achieved.

Indonesia has returned to the market with further green sukuk since, including retail issues for its own citizens.

**Lesson for a bank:** the same four components (use of proceeds, selection, management of proceeds and reporting) plus external review work for a sovereign and for a bank. Investors buy the discipline as much as the label.

cards.title: Green bond and green sukuk
cards.caption: Same green discipline, different legal structures.

items.label: What investors hold
items.left: A debt claim on the issuer
items.right: Ownership interests in underlying assets or a venture

items.label: Return comes from
items.left: Interest or coupon payments
items.right: Rent, profit or returns on the underlying assets

items.label: Extra approval
items.left: Not applicable
items.right: Shariah board approval of the structure

items.label: Green requirement
items.left: Proceeds go to eligible green projects
items.right: Same, and the underlying assets should be eligible too

cards.question: A fertiliser company issues a bond whose proceeds can be used for any purpose, but its profit rate rises if it misses a target to cut emissions per tonne by 2030. What kind of instrument is this?
options: A use-of-proceeds green bond
A green sukuk
A sustainability-linked instrument
A refinance scheme
cards.explanation: Sustainability-linked instruments are general-purpose funding whose terms depend on hitting performance targets. A use-of-proceeds green bond instead ring-fences the money for eligible green projects.

cards.back: An independent review, before issue, of whether a green framework is credible and in line with market principles.
Shows where the proceeds went: which project categories, how much, and how much is still unallocated.
Shows what the funded projects achieved, such as MWh of clean power generated or tonnes of CO₂ avoided, with the method used.
An official list of activities and criteria for what counts as green. The EU adopted one in 2020, ASEAN has published its own, and many countries are building theirs; check which applies.
How far back a framework allows existing loans to be refinanced with green proceeds. It should be stated and disclosed.
Claiming the same green asset or tonnes avoided twice, such as in two bonds or reports. When two lenders co-finance a plant, each should claim only its financing share of the impact.

cards.title: Real case: DWS fined over ESG claims (2023)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in **September 2023** the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced that DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank, would pay a **USD 19 million** penalty over misstatements about its ESG investment process. It paid a further, separate penalty over anti-money-laundering failings.

**The SEC's finding, in short:** DWS had marketed itself as a leader in ESG investing, but for several years did not adequately carry out parts of the ESG integration policy it had described to clients. DWS settled without admitting or denying the findings.

**Why it matters for green products:**
- Greenwashing is not only about labels on products. Saying you follow a process you do not follow is also misleading.
- Supervisors now treat sustainability claims like any other financial claim: they must be backed by evidence.
- Write down your green criteria, apply them every time, and keep the records.

cards.title: Keep the green book clean
cards.body:
- **Pay vendors directly** and match serial numbers to invoices.
- **Tag at origination**, using written criteria, not at year-end when someone needs a bigger number.
- **One asset, one claim.** Keep a register so the same solar plant is not counted in a sukuk pool and a separate green loan report.
- **Record the impact basis**: expected kWh, fuel saved or water saved, and how it was estimated.
- If a client's claim sounds too good, ask for the data before the brochure goes out.

cards.question: A textile mill spends USD 4 million on a waste-heat recovery system that cuts its gas bill by USD 1.6 million a year. What is the simple payback period?
options: 4.0 years
2.5 years
1.6 years
0.4 years
cards.explanation: Simple payback = cost ÷ annual saving = 4m ÷ 1.6m = 2.5 years. Dividing the other way gives 0.4, which is the share of the cost recovered each year, not the payback period.

cards.title: Solar Bazaar mastered
items: Green products include renewable energy, energy efficiency, green buildings, clean transport and water and waste projects; green needs evidence.
Central bank and development-bank refinance gives lenders cheap funding to lend at capped rates, but the bank keeps the credit risk; always check current scheme terms.
Payback = cost ÷ annual saving; check that savings cover the instalment before promising a self-paying loan.
Green bonds and sukuk rest on use of proceeds, evaluation and selection, management of proceeds and reporting, ideally with external review.
Sustainability-linked instruments tie terms to targets instead of ring-fencing proceeds.
Watch for vague claims, hidden trade-offs, 'lesser of two evils', unproven numbers, relabelling and double counting.

cards.prompt: Which of your customers could save money with a green upgrade such as solar, efficient motors or drip irrigation? What evidence would you need before you could honestly call that loan green?

quiz.question: A small shop's rooftop solar system costs USD 7,200 and is expected to save USD 200 a month on electricity and generator fuel. What is the simple payback period?
options: 28 months
45 months
25 months
36 months
quiz.explanation: Simple payback = cost ÷ monthly saving = 7,200 ÷ 200 = 36 months, or three years.

quiz.question: How does a central bank concessionary refinance scheme for renewable energy generally work?
options: The central bank lends directly to households and businesses for solar panels
The bank lends at normal market rates and the central bank repays the loan in full if the customer defaults within the scheme period
The central bank gives the bank low-cost refinance; the bank lends at a capped rate to eligible customers and keeps the credit risk
Vendors receive subsidies from the central bank and the bank is not involved
quiz.explanation: Refinance schemes channel cheap funding through banks, which lend on at capped end-user rates. The bank still assesses and carries the credit risk.

quiz.question: Which financing request best fits green lending criteria?
options: New diesel generators that burn slightly less fuel than the old ones
A new coal-fired boiler for a textile mill
General working capital for a company that says it loves the planet
Drip irrigation for an orchard, reducing water use
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers a clear environmental benefit by saving water. Slightly more efficient diesel generators and a new coal boiler lock in fossil fuel use, and a slogan is not a green purpose.

quiz.question: Which component of a green bond or sukuk framework covers how the issuer tracks proceeds and what it does with money not yet allocated?
options: Use of proceeds
Management of proceeds
Evaluation and selection
Impact reporting
quiz.explanation: Management of proceeds covers tracking through a sub-account or register and holding unallocated funds in stated instruments. Use of proceeds defines what the money may fund.

quiz.question: A bank's green sukuk of USD 800 million has USD 600 million allocated to eligible assets after one year. What should its allocation report show?
options: 100% allocated, because the full amount has been raised
75% allocated and USD 200 million unallocated, with where the unallocated funds are held
Only the impact achieved, because allocation details are commercially confidential to the bank
33% unallocated and no further detail
quiz.explanation: Allocated share = 600 ÷ 800 = 75%, leaving USD 200 million (25%) unallocated. A good report states both and explains how unallocated funds are held.

quiz.question: Before issuing its first green sukuk, Banyan Bridge asks an independent firm to assess whether its green framework is credible and in line with market principles. What is this called?
options: A second-party opinion
An impact report
An allocation report
A Shariah audit
quiz.explanation: A second-party opinion is an independent pre-issue review of the framework. Allocation and impact reports come after issuance, and a Shariah audit checks Shariah compliance, not green credentials.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a sustainability-linked instrument from a use-of-proceeds green bond?
options: Its proceeds must be spent only on solar projects
It can only be issued by a central bank
Its proceeds can fund general purposes, but its terms change with whether the issuer meets sustainability targets
It never includes any financial consequences for missing targets, so it works mainly as a public statement of intent
quiz.explanation: Sustainability-linked instruments are general-purpose funding with terms such as the profit rate tied to performance targets. A use-of-proceeds green bond ring-fences the money for eligible projects.

quiz.question: A factory advertises its new solar roof as proof it is a 'green company' while its untreated effluent still flows into a canal. Which form of greenwashing is this?
options: Lesser of two evils
Hidden trade-off
Relabelling
Double counting
quiz.explanation: Highlighting one green feature while hiding a significant harmful one is a hidden trade-off. Lesser of two evils is calling a slightly better polluting option green.

quiz.question: What is the key structural difference between a green sukuk and a green bond?
options: A green sukuk has no requirement for proceeds to go to green projects, because Shariah approval already covers the environmental side as well
A green bond needs Shariah board approval, while a sukuk does not
Sukuk holders own interests in underlying assets and earn returns from them; bondholders hold a debt claim earning interest
Sukuk can only be issued by foreign governments
quiz.explanation: Sukuk give investors interests in underlying assets, with returns from rent or profit, and need Shariah approval. Green requirements apply to both, and for sukuk the underlying assets should be eligible too.

quiz.question: Which control best prevents a solar loan from being used for something other than solar?
options: Asking the customer to sign a declaration that the whole amount will be used for solar equipment
Disbursing the full amount to the customer's account quickly
Paying the approved vendor directly and checking installation evidence against the invoice
Relying on the customer's past repayment record
quiz.explanation: Direct payment to the vendor plus installation evidence (certificate, photos, serial numbers) makes diversion very hard. A declaration or a good track record does not prove where the money went.

sessions.title: Own Impact, Islamic Alignment, Disclosure and the Green Banking Unit
sessions.summary: Three weeks to the board meeting. Measure the bank's own footprint across scopes 1, 2 and 3, connect sustainability to Islamic finance principles, plan honest climate disclosure, and design the green banking unit that will carry the mandate forward.
objectives: Classify a bank's emission sources into scopes 1, 2 and 3 and calculate them from activity data and emission factors
Estimate financed emissions using a simple attribution approach and explain why they usually dwarf a bank's own operations
Explain where Islamic finance principles support sustainability and where an extra ESG lens is still needed
Organise climate disclosure under four pillars and design a green banking unit with clear roles and reporting lines

cards.title: Do we walk the talk?
cards.setting: Board secretariat, group head office, Singapore. The agenda for the November board meeting is pinned to the wall.

lines.text: The board has read our risk work and loved the solar product. Now one director asks the awkward question: what is our own footprint?
Our footprint? We're a bank. We don't have chimneys.
We have 300 branches, many with diesel generators, a fleet of cars, a big electricity bill, and thousands of flights. And then there is everything we finance.
(joining from Dubai) And our Shariah board chair asked me something too: 'We run an Islamic window. Aren't we green by definition?' I wasn't sure how to answer.
Good questions, both. This is the Board Summit: measure ourselves honestly, answer the Shariah question properly, plan our disclosure and design the unit that keeps this going.

scenes.heading: Scope 1: what we burn
scenes.narration: Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources the bank owns or controls: diesel in branch generators, fuel in bank cars, and leaks of refrigerant gas from air conditioners.

scenes.heading: Scope 2: what we buy
scenes.narration: Scope 2 covers emissions from generating the electricity the bank buys from the grid. The power plant burns the fuel, but the bank's demand causes it.

scenes.heading: Scope 3: the value chain
scenes.narration: Scope 3 covers other indirect emissions: business flights, staff commuting, paper and supplies, waste, and, for a bank, the emissions of the borrowers and investments it finances.

scenes.heading: Financed emissions dominate
scenes.narration: For most banks, financed emissions are many times larger than everything else combined. That is where the real climate impact, and the transition risk, sits.

scenes.heading: The basic formula
scenes.narration: Most estimates use the same idea: activity data times an emission factor. Litres of diesel times kilograms of CO₂ per litre. Kilowatt-hours times kilograms per kilowatt-hour. Then divide by a thousand to get tonnes.

cards.title: Which scope?
cards.prompt: Sort each source in Banyan Bridge's footprint into the right scope.

items.text: Diesel burned in branch backup generators
Petrol used by the bank's own pool cars
Refrigerant gas leaking from branch air conditioners
Electricity bought from the grid for head office
Electricity bought from the grid for branches
Staff flights between Singapore and Dubai
Employees commuting in their own cars
Emissions of a fertiliser plant the bank has lent to
Paper bought for statements and forms

cards.title: Calculating a footprint
cards.body:
**Emissions = activity data × emission factor.**

Illustrative factors for practice (real work should use current official or recognised factors, which differ by source and year):
- Diesel: about **2.7 kg CO₂ per litre**.
- Petrol: about **2.3 kg CO₂ per litre**.
- Grid electricity: assume **0.45 kg CO₂ per kWh** (real grid factors differ by country and year with the fuel mix).

**Banyan Bridge, one year:**
- Generators: 450,000 litres × 2.7 = 1,215,000 kg = **1,215 t** (scope 1)
- Pool cars: 200,000 litres × 2.3 = 460,000 kg = **460 t** (scope 1)
- Electricity: 18,000,000 kWh × 0.45 = 8,100,000 kg = **8,100 t** (scope 2)

Scope 1 = 1,215 + 460 = **1,675 t**. Scopes 1 and 2 together = **9,775 t**.

Watch the units: **1 tonne = 1,000 kg**. Most errors in footprint reports are unit mistakes.

cards.title: Banyan Bridge's footprint at a glance
cards.caption: Illustrative figures using the practice factors. The single financed-emissions line already dwarfs the bank's own operations.

items.label: Scope 1
items.detail: Generator diesel (1,215 t) plus pool car petrol (460 t).

items.label: Scope 2
items.detail: 18 million kWh of grid electricity × 0.45 kg/kWh.

items.label: Avoidable with solar
items.detail: Solar on 50 branches producing 2 million kWh a year: 2,000,000 × 0.45 = 900,000 kg.

items.label: One borrower's financed share
items.detail: Just one fertiliser loan, about six times scopes 1 and 2 combined.

cards.question: A branch network uses 60,000 litres of diesel in generators in a year. Using 2.7 kg CO₂ per litre, what are the emissions and which scope do they fall in?
options: 162 tonnes, scope 1
162 tonnes, scope 2
162,000 tonnes, scope 1
22 tonnes, scope 3
cards.explanation: 60,000 × 2.7 = 162,000 kg = 162 tonnes. Fuel burned in equipment the bank owns is scope 1. Forgetting to divide by 1,000 gives the 162,000 figure, a classic unit error.

cards.title: Estimating financed emissions
cards.body:
A common approach (used by industry methods for financed emissions, such as the PCAF standard) attributes to the bank a **share of the borrower's emissions** equal to the bank's share of the borrower's financing.

**Attribution factor = bank's outstanding amount ÷ borrower's total equity + debt**

**Example: Delta Agro Fertilisers (fictional)**
- Banyan Bridge's outstanding loan: **USD 200 million**
- Company's total equity plus debt: **USD 4 billion**
- Attribution factor: 0.2 ÷ 4 = **5%**
- Company's scope 1 and 2 emissions: **1,200,000 t CO₂**
- Financed emissions: 1,200,000 × 5% = **60,000 t CO₂**

That one loan is about six times the bank's own scopes 1 and 2 (9,775 t). Data quality varies: reported emissions are best, estimates from production or sector averages are weaker, so methods ask banks to score and disclose data quality.

cards.title: The Shariah board's question
cards.setting: Islamic banking division, Dubai International Financial Centre. The Shariah board chair's question is written on the whiteboard: 'Are we green by definition?'

lines.text: Our Islamic window avoids interest, gambling and alcohol. Every deal is tied to a real asset. Surely that makes us sustainable already?
It gives us a strong foundation. Ideas like stewardship of the earth, no harm, and avoiding waste sit right at the heart of Islamic ethics.
But I checked our Islamic book. We have a diminishing musharakah for a coal-fired captive power unit. Fully Shariah-compliant. Not exactly green.
Exactly. Shariah screening asks whether a transaction is permissible. It does not automatically measure carbon or pollution. We need both lenses.
So the answer to our Shariah board chair is: our principles point towards sustainability, and an ESG lens helps us live up to them.

cards.back: Humans as trustees of the earth, not its owners. Resources are held in trust for others and for future generations.
Trust and responsibility. A financier is accountable for how entrusted wealth is used, including its effects on people and nature.
Balance. Creation has a natural balance that people should not disturb, a strong basis for protecting climate and ecosystems.
A legal maxim: no harm should be caused and none returned. Financing an activity that pollutes a village sits uneasily with it.
Wastefulness and excess, discouraged in Islamic teaching. Energy efficiency and waste reduction fit naturally with avoiding it.
The objectives of Shariah, including protecting life, intellect, lineage, wealth and faith. Climate harm threatens life and wealth across generations.

cards.title: Islamic finance and sustainable finance
cards.caption: Strong common ground, but Shariah compliance and climate alignment are different tests.

items.label: Real economy
items.left: Financing is tied to real assets and trade, not pure speculation
items.right: A real asset can still be a high-carbon or polluting one

items.label: Screening
items.left: Excludes impermissible sectors such as alcohol and gambling
items.right: Does not automatically exclude coal, deforestation or heavy pollution

items.label: Ethics
items.left: No harm, stewardship and avoiding waste are core values
items.right: Values need measurable E&S criteria to be applied deal by deal

items.label: Risk sharing
items.left: Partnership structures align the financier with the project's success
items.right: Shared risk includes climate risk, which still has to be measured

cards.question: Mei Lin finds a fully Shariah-compliant ijarah financing a fleet of old, highly polluting diesel trucks. What does this show?
options: The ijarah must be invalid under Shariah because it is polluting
Islamic finance has no connection with sustainability
Shariah compliance and environmental performance are separate tests, so an ESG lens is still needed
Diesel trucks are automatically excluded by Shariah screening
cards.explanation: Shariah screening asks whether a transaction is permissible; it does not automatically measure emissions or pollution. Islamic principles such as no harm support sustainability, but bringing them to life needs measurable E&S criteria alongside Shariah review.

cards.title: Four pillars of climate disclosure
cards.prompt: Amara drafts the bank's first climate report. Match each draft paragraph to the pillar it belongs under.

pairs.right: The board risk committee reviews climate risk every quarter, and the Head of Green Banking reports to it.
Under a flood scenario, agri losses could rise about fourfold; we are growing solar and adaptation finance in response.
Every corporate deal is screened for E&S risk and categorised; climate overlays feed into credit ratings.
Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 9,775 t; we aim to cut them 30% from this baseline by 2030.

cards.title: Disclosure in four pillars
cards.body:
Climate disclosure that investors and regulators recognise is usually organised in four pillars, first set out by the TCFD in 2017 and now built into the ISSB's IFRS S2 standard (2023):

- **Governance:** who oversees climate issues at board and management level, and how often.
- **Strategy:** the climate risks and opportunities the bank faces, their effect on its business and plans, and how resilient it is under different scenarios.
- **Risk management:** how the bank identifies, assesses and manages climate risk and fits it into its overall risk framework.
- **Metrics and targets:** the numbers used to track progress, such as scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, financed emissions and green financing volumes, and the targets set against a stated baseline.

Countries are adopting these standards at different speeds and often in phases: the UK, Singapore, Japan and others have moved ahead. Check what applies to your bank now.

cards.title: Real case: ASIC v Mercer, Australia (2024)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in **August 2024** Australia's Federal Court ordered Mercer Superannuation to pay a penalty of **AUD 11.3 million** in a case brought by the securities regulator, ASIC.

**The issue:** Mercer had described some of its 'Sustainable Plus' investment options as excluding companies involved in fossil fuels, alcohol and gambling. In fact those options held investments in such companies. Mercer admitted the statements were misleading.

**Why it matters for a bank's own claims:**
- It was ASIC's first greenwashing case to reach court, and regulators elsewhere have taken similar action.
- A sustainability claim is a statement of fact. If the portfolio does not match the words, the words are misleading.
- Before any public claim (green, sustainable, net zero), check that the data and the controls behind it actually exist.

cards.title: The CEO's headline
cards.situation: Two days before the board meeting, the CEO's office sends a draft press release: 'Banyan Bridge will be a net-zero bank by 2030.' The bank has measured scopes 1 and 2 for one year, has no financed-emissions baseline and no transition plan. What do you advise Amara to recommend?

choices.text: Publish it. A bold headline shows leadership and the details can be worked out later.
choices.outcome: The headline gets coverage, then an analyst points out that the bank's financed emissions are unmeasured and its loan book grew in carbon-heavy sectors. The claim looks like greenwashing and the bank spends a year defending it.

choices.text: Make the claim true by buying the cheapest carbon offsets available to cancel out scopes 1 and 2.
choices.outcome: Low-quality offsets do little to cut real emissions and are widely criticised. The claim still ignores financed emissions, the largest part of the footprint. Offsets can play a limited role after real reductions, not instead of them.

choices.text: Recommend a precise commitment instead: publish the scope 1 and 2 baseline, a reduction target with a plan (solar, efficiency), and a commitment to measure financed emissions before setting targets for them.
choices.outcome: The board agrees. The release is less flashy but every sentence can be backed by evidence, and investors welcome the clear baseline and next steps. Credible targets are specific, measured and honest about scope.

choices.text: Recommend saying nothing about climate at all until every number is perfect.
choices.outcome: This avoids overclaiming but leaves stakeholders guessing and wastes the work done so far. Honest disclosure of what is known, with clear limits, is better than silence.

cards.title: Building the Green Banking Unit
cards.caption: Amara's first-year plan for the board. Sequence matters more than speed.

items.label: Policy and mandate
items.detail: Board approves the green banking policy, exclusion list and the unit's reporting line.

items.label: People and training
items.detail: Hire E&S officers independent of business targets; train credit, branch and product staff.

items.label: Embed in credit
items.detail: Add E&S screening and categories to the credit workflow and approval forms.

items.label: Data and MIS
items.detail: Tag green loans, geo-code collateral, record emissions data and build the footprint inventory.

items.label: Products and own impact
items.detail: Launch solar and efficiency products; start branch solar and paperless projects.

items.label: Report
items.detail: First disclosure under four pillars; report to the board and to the supervisor as required.

cards.title: Real case: HSBC's climate adverts banned in the UK (2022)
cards.body:
**What happened:** in **October 2022** the UK's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) ruled that two HSBC posters shown in the UK were misleading and must not appear again in that form.

**The ads:** they highlighted the bank's plan to provide up to USD 1 trillion of financing and investment to help clients move to net zero, and a tree-planting project.

**The ruling, in short:** the ASA found the ads left out material information: that HSBC was still financing significant amounts of greenhouse-gas-emitting activity. Consumers could take away a misleading picture of the bank's overall climate impact.

**Lessons for disclosure:**
- What you leave out can mislead as much as what you say.
- Green financing targets need to sit next to an honest picture of financed emissions.
- Marketing and disclosure teams should work from the same verified numbers.

cards.title: Design the unit to be listened to
cards.body:
- **Independence:** E&S officers who sign off on deals should not report to, or be paid on targets set by, the business lines whose deals they review.
- **Seniority:** the head of the unit needs direct access to senior management and a board committee, or findings get buried.
- **Embedding:** the unit sets standards and reviews higher-risk deals; relationship managers still own the first screening.
- **Measure it:** track deals screened, action items closed, green financing volume and the bank's own footprint, and report them.

cards.question: A bank lends USD 150 million to a cement company whose total equity plus debt is USD 3 billion. The company emits 900,000 t CO₂ a year. Using the attribution approach, what are the bank's financed emissions from this loan?
options: 45,000 t CO₂
4,500 t CO₂
60,000 t CO₂
cards.explanation: Attribution factor = 150m ÷ 3,000m = 5%. Financed emissions = 900,000 × 5% = 45,000 t CO₂. Counting the company's full emissions would ignore that other financiers fund the other 95%.

cards.title: The Board Summit
cards.setting: Boardroom, Singapore. Eleven directors, one screen, and Amara's team waiting by the door.

lines.text: Amara presents: the flood stress test, the Kaveri tannery turnaround, the solar pipeline, the sukuk framework and the bank's first footprint.
I'll say this to the board directly. I called floods an act of God. I was wrong to stop there. Nile Ridge Cement is now working with us on a waste-heat project.
And the six districts: concentration is down, more loans have crop insurance or takaful cover, and early-warning calls saved stock in two branches last flood season.
The Shariah board has endorsed adding an E&S lens to Islamic products. Our principles and our practice now point the same way.
The board has renewed our mandate. One last step for you: the certification exam. Show them you can do all of this on your own.

cards.title: Board Summit complete
items: Scope 1 is fuel the bank burns, scope 2 is purchased electricity, scope 3 is the value chain, including financed emissions.
Emissions = activity × factor; divide kg by 1,000 for tonnes; use current recognised factors in real reports.
Financed emissions = borrower emissions × (bank's outstanding ÷ borrower's equity plus debt); they usually dwarf own operations.
Islamic principles such as khilafah, mizan and no harm support sustainability, but Shariah compliance does not by itself measure carbon or pollution.
Disclose under governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets; avoid headline claims you cannot back with a baseline and plan.
A green banking unit needs a board-approved mandate, independent E&S officers, embedded processes, data and regular reporting.

cards.prompt: If your own branch or department had to cut its scope 1 and 2 emissions by a third, what three changes would you propose first, and how would you measure whether they worked?

quiz.question: Diesel burned in a bank's branch backup generators falls under which emissions scope?
options: Scope 2
Scope 3
Scope 1
It is not counted, because generators are only for backup
quiz.explanation: Fuel burned in equipment the bank owns or controls is a direct, scope 1 emission. Backup use still counts.

quiz.question: Banyan Bridge's head office buys 4,000,000 kWh of grid electricity a year. Using 0.45 kg CO₂ per kWh, what are the emissions, and in which scope?
options: 1,800 tonnes, scope 1
1,800,000 tonnes, scope 2
180 tonnes, scope 3
1,800 tonnes, scope 2
quiz.explanation: 4,000,000 × 0.45 = 1,800,000 kg = 1,800 tonnes. Purchased electricity is scope 2. Forgetting to convert kg to tonnes gives 1,800,000.

quiz.question: For most banks, which category of emissions is usually the largest?
options: Generator diesel in scope 1
Financed emissions in scope 3
Purchased electricity in scope 2
Staff commuting in scope 3
quiz.explanation: The emissions of the borrowers and investments a bank finances are usually many times larger than its own operations. That is also where most transition risk sits.

quiz.question: A bank has USD 300 million outstanding to a steel company whose total equity plus debt is USD 5 billion. The company emits 400,000 t CO₂ a year. What are the bank's attributed financed emissions?
options: 2,400 t CO₂
24,000 t CO₂
quiz.explanation: Attribution factor = 300m ÷ 5,000m = 6%. Financed emissions = 400,000 × 6% = 24,000 t CO₂. Counting the company's full 400,000 t would ignore that other financiers fund the other 94%.

quiz.question: The Shariah board chair asks whether an Islamic window is automatically green. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Islamic principles support sustainability, but Shariah screening does not automatically exclude high-carbon or polluting activities
Yes, because all Shariah-compliant financing is green by definition, since every transaction must be tied to a real and productive asset
No, because Islamic finance has nothing to say about the environment
Yes, because Islamic finance avoids interest, and interest is the main cause of pollution
quiz.explanation: Concepts such as khilafah, mizan and no harm align closely with sustainability, but Shariah screening focuses on permissibility. A compliant deal can still finance a polluting asset, so measurable E&S criteria are needed alongside it.

quiz.question: Which Islamic legal maxim most directly supports refusing to finance an activity that would pollute a village's water supply?
options: Israf: avoiding wastefulness
Amanah: honesty in keeping deposits
La darar wa la dirar: no harm should be caused and none returned
Takaful: mutual insurance
quiz.explanation: The no-harm maxim speaks directly to activities that damage others. Israf concerns waste and excess, amanah concerns trust and responsibility, and takaful is a form of mutual cover.

quiz.question: A bank's climate report describes how its loan book would perform under a disorderly transition scenario and how it is shifting lending in response. Which disclosure pillar does this belong under?
options: Governance
Risk management
Strategy
Metrics and targets
quiz.explanation: Strategy covers climate risks and opportunities, their effects on the business and plans, and resilience under different scenarios. Risk management covers the processes for identifying and managing risk.

quiz.question: Which reporting line best protects the independence of a green banking unit's E&S officers?
options: To the relationship managers whose deals they review, since they understand the clients, the sectors and the business best
They report to the branch manager of each branch
They report only to the marketing department
To the head of the green banking unit, who has senior and board access, and not paid on business lending targets
quiz.explanation: E&S officers must be able to challenge deals without pressure from the people who earn from them. An independent line with senior and board access keeps their findings from being buried.

quiz.question: Staff flights between Singapore and Dubai for meetings fall under which emissions scope for the bank?
options: Scope 1
Scope 2
Scope 3
None, because the airline owns the aircraft
quiz.explanation: Business travel in vehicles the bank does not own is an indirect emission in its value chain, scope 3. The airline counts the fuel in its own scope 1.

quiz.question: The CEO wants to announce 'net zero by 2030' although only one year of scope 1 and 2 data exists and financed emissions have not been measured. What is the most credible alternative?
options: Publish the scope 1 and 2 baseline with a target and plan, and commit to measuring financed emissions before targeting them
Announce net zero and buy the cheapest available carbon offsets to cover all of scopes 1 and 2 until real reductions eventually arrive
Announce net zero and explain the details in five years
Remove scope 2 from the baseline to make the target easier
quiz.explanation: Credible commitments rest on a measured baseline, specific targets and a plan, and are honest about what is not yet measured. Cheap offsets or vague future details invite greenwashing criticism, and shrinking the baseline is misleading.

bank.question: After the floods, Banyan Bridge's Sylhet branch is under water for three weeks. Its ATMs are offline, staff cannot reach the building and customer records must be served from another city. Which risk does this most directly represent for the bank?
options: Credit risk, because borrowers near Sylhet will find it much harder to repay their loans while the branch is closed
Operational risk, because the bank's own premises, systems and people cannot function normally
Transition risk, because the bank will have to move its branch to a safer place
Market risk, because the value of the bank's investments may fall
bank.explanation: Damage to the bank's own branches, systems and staff access is operational risk. Credit risk will probably rise too, but the situation described is about the bank's ability to operate. Relocation is an adaptation choice, not transition risk, which concerns the shift to a low-carbon economy.

bank.question: A cement producer in North Africa exports a growing share of its output to Europe. The EU begins charging importers for the carbon embedded in cement. How should the producer's lender describe this risk?
options: A chronic physical risk, because cement plants contribute to rising temperatures
A liability risk, because the EU is taking the producer to court
Not a risk for the lender, because the charge is paid in Europe
A policy-driven transition risk that can reduce the borrower's export margins and cash flow
bank.explanation: A border carbon charge is a policy response to the low-carbon transition, so it is transition risk. It reaches the lender because it squeezes the exporter's margins or volumes. Nobody is suing the producer, and the fact that the charge is levied abroad does not stop it from hitting the borrower's cash flow.

bank.question: Over twenty years, the water table under a group of apple orchards in a dry inland valley has fallen steadily, pushing up pumping costs and cutting yields. The orchards secure several loans. How is this risk best classified?
options: Acute physical risk
Chronic physical risk
Technology transition risk
Reputational risk
bank.explanation: A slow, persistent decline in water availability is chronic physical risk. An acute risk would be a sudden event such as a flash flood or a single heatwave.

bank.question: A ceramic tile maker runs coal-fired kilns. Mei Lin is listing the outside-in climate factors for its credit file. Which item belongs on that list?
options: The smoke from the kilns that affects the health of workers' families living nearby
Expected increases in fuel costs and possible carbon rules that would raise the company's production costs
The company's contribution to its country's national greenhouse gas emissions, which is reported in the national inventory every few years
Complaints from a neighbouring village about ash dumped on common land
bank.explanation: Outside-in factors are climate and ESG issues that affect the borrower's own business, such as rising fuel costs and carbon rules. The smoke, ash and emissions are inside-out impacts on people and the environment. Those can later become outside-in risks through fines or protests, but as described they are the company's impacts, not risks to it.

bank.question: Banyan Bridge has four exposures of similar size. Which one is most likely to become a stranded-asset problem for the bank?
options: A 15-year term loan for a new fuel-oil power plant selling to the grid
A one-year working capital line for a cotton trader
A five-year lease for rooftop solar panels on a hospital
A short-term import finance line for a pharmaceutical distributor
bank.explanation: Stranded assets lose value before the end of their expected life because of transition forces. A long-tenor loan to a fossil-fuel plant gives cheaper renewables and tighter rules years to make the plant uneconomic while debt is still outstanding. The short-term lines turn over quickly, and solar is on the winning side of the transition.

bank.question: In the month after the floods, deposits at Banyan Bridge's branches in flood-hit districts fall sharply as customers withdraw savings to repair homes and buy seed. Which risk does this mainly create for the bank?
options: Credit risk, because the depositors may default on their loans
Transition risk, because customers are moving to greener banks
Liquidity risk, because the bank must meet a sudden outflow of deposits
Operational risk, because the branches cannot open
bank.explanation: A sudden fall in deposits tests the bank's ability to meet outflows, which is liquidity risk. The customers are depositors withdrawing their own money, not borrowers defaulting, and nothing suggests they are switching banks for green reasons.

bank.question: A pharmaceutical company has excellent waste treatment and safety records. However, its CEO also chairs the board's audit committee, and the company recently bought land from the CEO's brother at well above market price. What should the credit team conclude from an ESG point of view?
options: The company is low ESG risk overall, because its excellent environmental and safety records outweigh a single board arrangement
There is a significant governance weakness that could hide losses or divert cash, despite strong environmental performance
The issue is social, because the land purchase affects the community
ESG review is not needed because pharmaceutical companies are low-emission
bank.explanation: A CEO overseeing the audit of his own management, plus a related-party deal above market price, is a governance red flag. Strong environmental results do not cancel it out: governance failures can drain cash from the company that owes the bank. ESG covers all three pillars, whatever the sector's emissions.

bank.question: A national newspaper reports that a housing project financed by Banyan Bridge displaced several hundred villagers on the edge of a fast-growing city without fair compensation. Protests have halted construction. Which statement best describes the bank's position?
options: This is purely the developer's problem, because the bank did not displace anyone and the loan instalments are still being paid on time
This is a chronic physical risk, because the land is changing use
A social issue in the project has created reputational risk for the bank and credit risk through construction delays
This is only a reputational issue, because the loan is still being repaid
bank.explanation: Unfair displacement is a social impact (inside-out) that is now hurting the borrower through halted construction, which raises credit risk, while the bank's name in the press is reputational risk. Lenders are judged by what they finance, and delays threaten repayment even if instalments are current today.

bank.question: Mei Lin compares two loans: a one-year crop finance line to a cotton grower in a flood-prone district, and a 15-year loan to a new coal-based captive power unit at a cement plant. Which statement about their climate exposure is most accurate?
options: Only the power loan has climate risk, because a one-year loan is repaid before any climate effect, physical or transition, can realistically occur
Only the crop line has climate risk, because transition risk takes centuries to appear
The crop line faces physical risk from the very next rainy season, while the long power loan lives long enough to be hit by transition changes as well
Both face the same climate risk because they are in the same country
bank.explanation: Tenor matters. A one-year agricultural loan can be hit by a single bad season. A 15-year loan to a coal-based asset is exposed to physical events too, but its long life also gives policy, technology and market shifts time to make the asset uneconomic while debt is outstanding.

bank.question: A board member asks for one sentence summarising how the floods affected Banyan Bridge. Which answer is most complete and accurate?
options: Some agriculture loans in flood-hit districts were rescheduled, which is a normal credit event handled through the usual process, with no wider effect on the bank or its customers
Borrowers' defaults rose and collateral lost value, branches and systems were disrupted, deposits were withdrawn, and the bank's response is being watched by stakeholders
The bank's carbon footprint rose because branches ran generators during the floods
Only borrowers whose own property was flooded were affected
bank.explanation: A climate event reaches the bank through several channels at once: credit (higher default probability and lower recoveries), operations, liquidity and reputation. Rescheduling describes only part of the credit response, and borrowers who stayed dry were also hit through second-round effects.

bank.question: A year later, Kaveri Leather Works asks for USD 300,000 to buy delivery vans and refurbish its sales office in Chennai. Its tannery action plan still has two open items. What is the most appropriate E&S approach?
options: Screen and categorise based on the vans and office, which have limited impacts, while tracking the open tannery actions in the file
Classify it as category A, because the client is a tannery and tanneries are always high risk
Skip E&S screening, because the client has already been through due diligence once
Decline until every tannery issue has been permanently resolved, whatever the new facility is for, because the client relationship is a single risk
bank.explanation: Categorisation follows the impacts of the activity financed, and vans plus an office refurbishment have limited impacts. The client relationship still matters, so open actions on the main plant stay on the radar. Skipping screening ignores the rule that every deal is screened, and an automatic A or a blanket decline ignores what is actually being financed.

bank.question: A new chemical blending plant is planned beside a river on the edge of an industrial city. The borrower has not yet shared details of its waste water or chemical storage, and the E&S officer cannot tell whether impacts are limited or significant. What should the officer do?
options: Assign the higher provisional category and let due diligence show whether a lower one is justified
Assign category C until the borrower provides information
Decline immediately, because missing information always means exclusion
Let the relationship manager choose the category, because he knows the client's operations and history best
bank.explanation: When impacts are uncertain, the safer practice is to choose the higher category and let evidence bring it down. Starting at C would let a potentially serious deal through with minimal checks. Missing information calls for more due diligence, not automatic exclusion, and categorisation should not be left to the person who earns from the deal.

bank.question: A dyeing unit's environmental approval covers two production lines. The bank is asked to finance two additional lines on the same plot, doubling output. What should the credit approval include?
options: Nothing extra, because the plot already has an approval
A covenant requiring the borrower to apply for an updated approval within five years of the first disbursement
A condition precedent that the borrower obtain approval covering the expanded capacity before disbursement
A requirement that the bank itself apply to the environmental authority on the borrower's behalf
bank.explanation: The existing approval does not cover the expansion, so approval for the new capacity should be a condition precedent: no money moves until it exists. A distant covenant leaves the bank financing an unapproved activity, and applying for approvals is the borrower's responsibility, not the bank's.

bank.question: The E&S assessment submitted for a steel re-rolling mill is signed by the mill's own environment manager and contains whole paragraphs that mention a different city. What is the best response?
options: Accept it, because the borrower is responsible for its own documents
Treat it as a red flag, ask for clarification and an independent assessment, and verify key points on a site visit
Decline the deal immediately, because submitting a misleading document is on its own enough reason to end the relationship
Ignore the report and categorise the deal as C to save time
bank.explanation: A report signed by the borrower's own staff and visibly copied from a template is a classic red flag. The right response is to ask more and verify, not to accept blindly. An immediate decline jumps to a conclusion before the borrower can explain, and downgrading to C to save time is the opposite of what the evidence suggests.

bank.question: Why does Amara prefer to release Kaveri Leather Works' loan in tranches tied to verified treatment upgrades, rather than all at once with a covenant to upgrade?
options: Tranching lowers the profit rate the borrower pays
Banking regulators prohibit releasing any business loan in a single disbursement
Covenants on environmental matters cannot be included in loan documents for category B deals under international standards
Tranching keeps the bank's leverage until each fix is verified; money already released cannot be held back
bank.explanation: Once the full amount is disbursed, a covenant breach gives the bank fewer practical options. Linking each tranche to verified progress keeps an incentive in place until the work is done. Tranching is a structuring choice, not a pricing tool or a blanket legal rule.

bank.question: A banking supervisor's inspection team asks Banyan Bridge for evidence that its green banking arrangements are properly governed. Which evidence best answers that request?
options: A large number of solar and energy-efficiency loans disbursed last year, showing strong growth in green business
Photos of tree-planting events organised by branch staff
A board-approved green banking policy, a designated green banking function with trained staff, and reporting records
A signed statement from the CEO to all staff confirming that the bank cares deeply about the environment and climate
bank.explanation: National green banking frameworks look for governance: a board-approved policy, a dedicated function, training and reporting. Solar loan volumes show green business activity, and tree planting or statements of intent do not show that risk is governed.

bank.question: A large coastal tourism resort involving land reclamation is presented with only a lighter, screening-level environmental approval. Mei Lin thinks a project of this scale would normally need a full EIA with public consultation. What should the bank do?
options: Proceed, because any approval from an environmental authority is enough for the bank
Commission and pay for a full EIA itself, then submit it to the authority on the borrower's behalf to save time
Treat it as a gap: check the local rules and ask the borrower to confirm the right level of assessment was done
Reclassify the project as category C, because it already has an approval
bank.explanation: A bank should check that the approval matches the project's scale and impacts. If a project of this kind would normally require a full EIA with public consultation, a lighter approval is a gap to resolve before financing. The bank does not replace the regulator, and having an approval says nothing about the E&S category.

bank.question: A borrower is building a 60-bed private hospital in Nairobi. Which set of E&S issues should due diligence focus on most?
options: Carbon emissions from patients' cars and the hospital's marketing budget
Resettlement of villages and loss of biodiversity in a river valley
Handling and disposal of medical waste, waste water, and worker health and safety
None, because hospitals are socially beneficial and need no E&S review
bank.explanation: A mid-sized hospital's main E&S risks are infectious and chemical medical waste, waste water and staff safety. These are limited and manageable, typical of category B. Resettlement is a feature of large infrastructure, and social benefit does not remove operating risks.

bank.question: Amara's team can make 60 site visits this year. Which allocation best reflects a risk-based monitoring approach?
options: Visit every borrower in turn, starting with the oldest relationships, so that no client is ever left unvisited
Visit category C borrowers first, because they are the most numerous
Spread visits equally across all branches, regardless of the deals they hold, so every region gets the same attention
Focus on category A deals and B deals with open actions, with lighter reviews for B deals whose actions are closed
bank.explanation: Monitoring effort should follow risk: the deals with the largest potential impacts and those with unfinished fixes need the most attention. Rotating by age, counting by number or spreading evenly by branch ignores where the risk sits.

bank.question: Which of the following would typically appear on a bank's E&S exclusion list?
options: Trade in protected wildlife species
Construction of a mid-sized hospital
Expansion of a poultry farm
Working capital for a software house
bank.explanation: Exclusion lists cover activities the bank will not finance at all, such as trade in protected wildlife, banned chemicals or forced labour. The other activities can be financed after normal categorisation and due diligence.

bank.question: Mei Lin stresses a USD 80 million cotton ginning portfolio. Probability of default rises from 1.5% to 4% and loss given default from 35% to 50%. By how much does expected loss increase?
options: USD 1.60 million
USD 0.42 million
USD 2.00 million
USD 1.18 million
bank.explanation: Baseline EL = 80m × 0.015 × 0.35 = 0.42m. Stressed EL = 80m × 0.04 × 0.50 = 1.60m. The increase is 1.60 − 0.42 = USD 1.18 million. USD 1.60 million is the stressed total, not the increase.

bank.question: Agricultural land valued at USD 24 million secures a loan of USD 18 million. Flood mapping places it in a high-hazard zone, so the bank applies a 40% haircut. How much additional collateral value is needed to restore 100% cover?
options: USD 6.0 million
USD 9.6 million
None, because the land is still worth more than the loan
USD 3.6 million
bank.explanation: Haircut value = 24m × 0.60 = 14.4m. To cover the 18m loan fully, the bank needs 18 − 14.4 = USD 3.6 million more. USD 9.6 million is the size of the haircut, and the unadjusted value is no longer the right basis once the hazard is recognised.

bank.question: In the common four-family framing of climate scenarios, which two families involve high physical risk?
options: Hot house world and too little, too late
Orderly and disorderly
Disorderly and too little, too late
Orderly and hot house world
bank.explanation: Physical risk is high where action is weak or insufficient: the hot house world and too little, too late. Orderly and disorderly scenarios assume enough action to keep physical damage relatively contained; disorderly is high on transition risk instead.

bank.question: A steel re-rolling mill has EBITDA of USD 24 million and annual interest of USD 8 million. Its emissions are 120,000 t CO₂ a year, and a disorderly scenario assumes it absorbs a carbon cost of USD 100 per tonne. What is the stressed interest cover?
bank.explanation: Carbon cost = 120,000 × 100 = USD 12 million. Stressed EBITDA = 24 − 12 = 12 million. Interest cover = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5×, down from 3.0×.

bank.question: The weather service forecasts very heavy rain over the delta next week. Banyan Bridge's agri team calls borrowers to advise them to move stored rice and seed to higher ground. Which stage of the credit cycle is this?
options: Origination, because the bank is contacting borrowers
Rating, because the borrowers' grades will change
Monitoring, using weather warnings as early-warning triggers
Portfolio limits, because the calls cover many borrowers
bank.explanation: Using weather alerts to act on existing exposures is monitoring. Origination is about new deals, rating is about assigning grades, and portfolio limits are about how much exposure the bank allows in a sector or district.

bank.question: In a flood stress test, one farmer cooperative has crop insurance and stores its harvest in raised warehouses, while a similar cooperative has neither. How should the analysis treat the first cooperative?
options: Assume a smaller rise in PD and LGD, because insurance and raised storage reduce income loss and protect collateral
Treat both the same, because they are in the same district
Exclude the first cooperative from the test entirely
Assume a larger rise in PD, because the insurance premiums and storage costs reduce the cooperative's spare cash every season
bank.explanation: Adaptation and risk transfer are genuine mitigants. Insurance or takaful supports cash flow after a loss and raised storage protects stock, so both PD and LGD should rise less. Ignoring mitigants would overstate risk; excluding the borrower would hide it.

bank.question: A rice exporter has a USD 5 million working capital limit and has drawn USD 3 million. Mei Lin's flood stress assumes the exporter draws the full limit during the crisis. Which input to expected loss is she changing?
options: Probability of default
Loss given default
Exposure at default
The collateral haircut
bank.explanation: Borrowers tend to draw their unused lines in a crisis, so the amount owed at default rises. Assuming a full drawdown raises EAD from USD 3 million to USD 5 million.

bank.question: The board asks: 'Could any of our power-sector loans become stranded before they mature?' Most of these loans run for 12 to 18 years. Which analysis design answers that question best?
options: A one-year flood stress test on the agriculture book, since floods were the bank's biggest recent climate loss
A top-down heat-stress analysis of the SME portfolio
A review of last year's provisions on power-sector loans
A long-horizon transition scenario covering the loans' remaining life, done bottom-up for the largest plants
bank.explanation: Stranding is a transition question that plays out over many years, so the horizon must match the loans' remaining life, and the large, distinct plants deserve borrower-level analysis. A one-year flood test or an SME heat analysis answers different questions, and last year's provisions look backwards.

bank.question: Two banks each hold USD 1 billion of agri loans with similar default probabilities. Bank A has 35% of its book in six neighbouring flood-prone districts; Bank B is spread across 30 districts. Why is Bank A's position riskier?
options: One flood can hit many of Bank A's borrowers at the same time, so losses come together instead of being spread out
Bank A's borrowers must have weaker financial statements
Bank B will never suffer flood losses
Concentration only matters for corporate loans, because agriculture losses are always spread across many small farmers
bank.explanation: Concentration means a single hazard can affect a large share of the book at once, which is why banks set limits by district and sector. Identical default probabilities do not help if defaults all happen together. Bank B can still suffer losses, just less concentrated ones.

bank.question: Which statement about climate scenarios is accurate?
options: They predict the single most likely climate outcome for the next year, which is why supervisors require them
They are plausible what-if pictures of the future used to test resilience, not predictions
They are only useful once borrowers report perfect emissions data
They replace the bank's normal credit analysis
bank.explanation: Scenarios explore what could happen under different assumptions so the bank can test its resilience. They are not forecasts, they can start with proxies, and they add to normal credit analysis rather than replacing it.

bank.question: A denim mill's gas bill is USD 12 million a year. A new high-efficiency boiler costing USD 6.5 million is expected to cut gas use by 18%. What is the simple payback period?
options: About 3.0 years
About 0.5 years
About 5.4 years
About 1.8 years
bank.explanation: Annual saving = 12m × 0.18 = USD 2.16 million. Payback = 6.5 ÷ 2.16 ≈ 3.0 years. Dividing the cost by the whole gas bill (6.5 ÷ 12) gives about 0.5, which wrongly assumes the boiler removes the entire bill.

bank.question: A Lagos workshop's solar system would save about USD 280 a month. The proposed financing gives an instalment of USD 330 a month. The customer has been told the loan 'pays for itself'. What should Layla do?
options: Correct the claim and restructure, for example with a bigger down payment, longer tenor or smaller system
Proceed as proposed, because the difference is small
Decline, because banking rules require every solar loan instalment to be fully covered by the expected monthly savings
Increase the savings estimate to USD 330 so the numbers match
bank.explanation: Before promising a self-paying loan, the bank should check that expected savings cover the instalment. Here they do not, so the honest course is to correct the claim and adjust the structure. Inflating the savings estimate is misleading, and a shortfall calls for restructuring, not an automatic decline.

bank.question: Treasury wants to include solar loans made six years ago in a new green sukuk's asset pool. What is the right way to handle this?
options: Include any loan the bank has ever called green, because older loans have already proven their environmental benefit over several years
Exclude all existing loans, because green proceeds may only finance new projects
Include them but leave refinancing out of the allocation report
Include them only if they meet the criteria and the framework's look-back period allows it, and disclose the refinancing share
bank.explanation: Refinancing existing eligible assets is common, but the framework should state the look-back period and the issuer should disclose how much is refinancing. Including loans without checking criteria is relabelling, a blanket ban is not required, and hiding refinancing undermines the report.

bank.question: Which set of metrics is most suitable for the impact report on a portfolio of rooftop solar loans?
options: Number of branches that sold the product, and the sales bonuses paid to staff for originating green loans
Total profit earned by the bank on the portfolio
Annual MWh of clean electricity generated and estimated tonnes of CO₂ avoided, with the method and factors used
Number of customer complaints about installation delays
bank.explanation: Impact reports show what funded projects achieved for the environment, such as clean energy generated and emissions avoided, along with the method. Sales and profit figures are business metrics, and complaints are service data.

bank.question: A 2 MW solar plant financed by Banyan Bridge sits in its green sukuk pool. A partner bank that co-financed the plant also counts the whole plant's CO₂ savings in its own green report, and Banyan Bridge's retail team adds the same plant to its separate green loan statistics. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: Double counting; keep a register so each asset and its impact is claimed once, and split co-financed impact by share
Hidden trade-off; stop reporting impact for solar plants
Relabelling; remove the plant from the sukuk pool and report it only in the retail team's green loan statistics instead
No problem, because the plant is genuinely green
bank.explanation: The same asset and the same tonnes avoided are being claimed several times, which overstates impact. A green asset register prevents repeat claims inside the bank, and co-financed impact is usually attributed by financing share. The plant is genuinely green, but its benefit cannot be counted more than once.

bank.question: A rival bank launches a 'green home loan' and says every home it finances is green. Its only criterion is that the house has at least one solar-powered light. What is the main weakness, and how should Banyan Bridge design its own product differently?
options: There is no weakness, because any solar equipment makes a home green
The claim is vague and unproven; tie eligibility to clear energy and water criteria, ideally a recognised green building standard, and verify them
The weakness is the interest rate; offer a lower rate instead
The weakness is the solar light; ban all solar equipment from home loans
bank.explanation: A single solar light does not make a home energy- or water-efficient, so the green label is vague and unsupported. A credible product defines measurable criteria, ideally linked to a recognised green building standard, and checks them. Pricing does not fix a misleading label.

bank.question: A relationship manager tells a factory owner exactly how much he will earn for each unit of surplus solar power he exports to the grid, based on rules he learned several years ago. What is the risk?
options: There is no risk, because grid export rates are fixed by law for 25 years from the date the system is first connected to the grid
Grid-export rules are set by energy regulators and are often revised, so the promised income may be wrong; check the current rules first
The risk is only that the panels may be stolen
The factory owner, not the bank, sets the export rate
bank.explanation: Net-metering, feed-in and other grid-export rules are revised in many countries, so quoting old terms can overstate savings and mislead the customer about affordability. The bank should base savings on the current rules and say what is uncertain.

bank.question: A customer asks for 'the central bank solar rate'. The branch manager remembers a rate from a training session three years ago. What is the correct response?
options: Quote the remembered rate, because refinance rates are permanent
Tell the customer such schemes have been abolished everywhere
Offer the remembered rate now to keep the customer, and adjust it later if the current scheme rules turn out to be different
Check the current scheme rules and the bank's available allocation before quoting any rate, limit or eligibility
bank.explanation: Refinance scheme rates, limits and eligibility are revised over time, and the bank's available allocation also matters. Quoting from memory risks misleading the customer. Nothing suggests the scheme has been abolished; that also needs checking.

bank.question: Banyan Bridge plans an ijarah-based green sukuk. The proceeds will fund solar loans, but the underlying asset leased to investors is the bank's existing head office building, which has no green features. How should Amara advise?
options: There is no issue, because only the use of proceeds matters for a sukuk
It is weaker than it could be: green sukuk are expected to have eligible underlying assets too, so use green assets or disclose clearly
The sukuk is invalid under Shariah because the building is not green
Replace the sukuk with a sustainability-linked loan, which avoids any external review of the underlying assets and the use of proceeds
bank.explanation: For green sukuk, investors and reviewers look at both the use of proceeds and the underlying assets. A non-green underlying asset invites greenwashing questions even if the proceeds are well used. Green features are not a Shariah validity condition, and switching instruments to avoid review misses the point.

bank.question: Which arrangement best reflects the 'evaluation and selection' component of a green sukuk framework?
options: A committee including the green unit and risk applies written eligibility and E&S criteria to choose pool assets
The treasury team adds any loan that helps reach the sukuk's target size, then asks the green unit to confirm it later
Investors vote on each asset after the sukuk is issued
The bank picks assets after the impact report is published
bank.explanation: Evaluation and selection means a documented process and responsible people applying written criteria, including E&S risk checks. Choosing assets to hit a size target or after reporting defeats the purpose.

bank.question: A regional bank burns 80,000 litres of diesel in branch generators and 40,000 litres of petrol in its own cars, and buys 2,500,000 kWh of grid electricity. Using 2.7 kg CO₂ per litre of diesel, 2.3 kg per litre of petrol and 0.45 kg per kWh, what are its scope 1 emissions?
options: 1,433 tonnes
308 tonnes
216 tonnes
308,000 tonnes
bank.explanation: Diesel: 80,000 × 2.7 = 216,000 kg = 216 t. Petrol: 40,000 × 2.3 = 92,000 kg = 92 t. Scope 1 = 216 + 92 = 308 t. Electricity (2,500,000 × 0.45 = 1,125 t) is scope 2; adding it gives 1,433 t, which is scopes 1 and 2 together. 308,000 is the figure in kilograms.

bank.question: Banyan Bridge installs rooftop solar on 30 branches. Each produces 25,000 kWh a year that would otherwise have come from the grid. Using 0.45 kg CO₂ per kWh, by how much do the bank's scope 2 emissions fall?
options: 750 tonnes
337,500 tonnes
33.75 tonnes
337.5 tonnes
bank.explanation: Total generation = 30 × 25,000 = 750,000 kWh. Avoided emissions = 750,000 × 0.45 = 337,500 kg = 337.5 tonnes. 750 confuses MWh with tonnes, and 337,500 is the answer in kilograms.

bank.question: A bank has two corporate loans. Loan A: USD 400 million to a company with total equity plus debt of USD 8 billion and emissions of 2,000,000 t CO₂. Loan B: USD 100 million to a company with total equity plus debt of USD 1 billion and emissions of 150,000 t CO₂. What are the bank's total attributed financed emissions from the two loans?
options: 11,500 t CO₂
bank.explanation: Loan A: 0.4 ÷ 8 = 5%, so 2,000,000 × 5% = 100,000 t. Loan B: 0.1 ÷ 1 = 10%, so 150,000 × 10% = 15,000 t. Total = 115,000 t. Adding the companies' full emissions (2,150,000 t) ignores that other financiers fund the rest.

bank.question: Which of these sources counts as a scope 1 emission for a bank?
options: Grid electricity used to run its data centre
Emissions of a textile mill it finances
Fuel burned by employees driving their own cars to work
Refrigerant gas leaking from air conditioners in its own branches
bank.explanation: Leaks from equipment the bank owns or controls are direct emissions, so they are scope 1. Grid electricity is scope 2, and financed emissions and staff commuting are scope 3.

bank.question: A draft footprint report states: 'Branch generators used 450,000 litres of diesel at 2.7 kg CO₂ per litre, producing 1,215,000 tonnes of CO₂.' What is wrong?
options: The factor should be applied per kWh, not per litre
Generator emissions belong in scope 2, so the number should be removed
The result is in kilograms; it should be 1,215 tonnes
Nothing is wrong; the figure is correct
bank.explanation: 450,000 × 2.7 = 1,215,000 kg, which is 1,215 tonnes once divided by 1,000. The litre-based factor is right for fuel, and generator diesel is scope 1. Unit slips like this overstate a footprint a thousandfold.

bank.question: Banyan Bridge's climate report states: 'We aim to raise green financing to 10% of new corporate lending by 2028; this year it reached 4%.' Under which disclosure pillar does this belong?
options: Governance
Strategy
Metrics and targets
Risk management
bank.explanation: A quantified target with a baseline and progress figure belongs under metrics and targets. Strategy explains how risks and opportunities affect the business plan; governance describes oversight; risk management describes processes.

bank.question: The Islamic banking division proposes a diminishing musharakah to finance a new coal-fired captive power unit for a textile group. The Shariah board has approved the structure. How should the green banking unit treat the deal?
options: Apply the same E&S and climate review as for a conventional deal; Shariah approval does not address emissions or stranding
Approve it as green, because Shariah-compliant financing is green by definition
Decline it, because Shariah screening automatically prohibits coal
Exclude it from the financed-emissions inventory, because a partnership is not a loan and so falls outside the calculation entirely
bank.explanation: Shariah approval confirms permissibility, not environmental performance. A long-life coal asset carries emissions and stranding risk, so it needs the same E&S and climate review as a conventional deal. Coal is not automatically prohibited by Shariah screening, and financed emissions apply to Islamic structures too.

bank.question: For its first financed-emissions estimate, Banyan Bridge has reported emissions for its 20 largest corporate borrowers but only sector averages for 5,000 SME borrowers. What is the best way to present this?
options: Report the estimate with a clear data-quality note for each part, and improve data for the largest estimated exposures first
Report only the 20 corporates and leave the SMEs out until perfect data exists, so the total is not distorted by rough estimates
Present all figures as equally reliable to avoid confusing readers
Delay any disclosure until every SME reports its own emissions
bank.explanation: Financed-emissions methods expect banks to use the best available data, score its quality and disclose it. Leaving out SMEs understates the total, presenting estimates as reported data misleads, and waiting for perfect data means never reporting.

bank.question: Three months into building the green banking unit, the marketing team wants to launch a solar product and a press campaign before E&S screening has been added to credit approvals or a board policy approved. What should Amara advise?
options: Launch the campaign now, because products and visibility matter more than policy in the first year of any new unit's life
Stop all green products until the first annual report is published
Let marketing write the green banking policy so it matches the campaign
Get the board-approved policy and mandate first and embed screening in credit, so green claims rest on working controls
bank.explanation: The build order matters: mandate and policy first, then people and embedding in credit, then products and reporting. Launching public green claims without controls invites greenwashing risk. Stopping everything is unnecessary, and policy should not be drafted by the team promoting the product.

bank.question: A director suggests the bank simply buy carbon offsets to become 'carbon neutral' instead of investing in branch solar and efficiency. What is the soundest response?
options: Offsets are always better than reductions because they are cheaper
Offsets are banned for banks under international climate standards
Offsets automatically cover financed emissions too, so buying enough of them solves the bank's entire footprint, operations and lending, in a single step
Offsets can cover what remains after real reductions, but cheap offsets used instead of cutting emissions invite greenwashing claims
bank.explanation: Credible climate plans cut emissions first and use good-quality offsets only for what remains. Using cheap offsets instead of reductions is widely criticised. Offsets are not banned, and buying them for operations does nothing about financed emissions.
